7.29 Search and Explore Available Products
Create a list indexed by product name to make it easier to query a specific product.

# divides information from each product.
divided_products <- split(fromJSON(all_Prods), seq(nrow(fromJSON(all_Prods))))
# Create a list indexed by the product name and version
products <- setNames(divided_products,fromJSON(all_Prods)$ProductAndVersion)
# Print no. products available in AppEEARS
sprintf("AppEEARS currently supports %i products." ,length(products))   

[1] "AppEEARS currently supports 193 products."


Next, look at the product’s names and descriptions. Below, the ‘ProductAndVersion’ and ‘Description’ are printed for all products.

# Loop through the products in the list and Print the product name and description
for (p in products){                                   
  print(paste0(p$ProductAndVersion," is ",p$Description," from ",p$Source))  
}

7.31 Submit an Area Request
The Submit task API call provides a way to submit a new request to be processed. It can accept data via JSON or query string. In the example below, create a JSON object and submit a request. Tasks in AppEEARS correspond to each request associated with your user account. Therefore, each of the calls to this service requires an authentication token.


7.31.1 Load a Shapefile
In this section, we load a shapefile using the sf package. The shapefile is publicly available for download from theNPS website.

nps <- st_read(

    layer = "nps_boundary"

text:
7.33 Compile a JSON Object
In this section, begin by setting up the information needed for a nested data list that will be later converted to a JSON object for submitting an AppEEARS area request.For detailed information on required JSON parameters, see the API Documentation.

taskName <- 'NEON-ONAQ'    # Enter name of the task, 'ONAQ' used here
taskType <- 'area'            # Type of task, it can be either "area" or "point"

projection <- projection$Name # Set output projection 

outFormat <- 'geotiff'        # Set output file format type. it can be either 'geotiff' or 'netcdf4'

startDate <- '01-01-2018'     # Start of the date range for which to extract data: MM-DD-YYYY
endDate <- '12-31-2019'       # End of the date range for which to extract data: MM-DD-YYYY
recurring <- FALSE            # Specify True for a recurring date range
#yearRange = [2000,2016]      # If recurring = True, set yearRange, change start/end date to MM-DD

To be able to successfully submit a task, the JSON object should be structured in a certain way. The code chunk below uses the information from the previous chunk to create a nested data frame. This nested data frame will be converted to JSON object that can be used to complete the request.

# Create a data frame including the date range for the request
date <- data.frame(startDate = startDate, endDate = endDate)

# Create a list including the projection and add the output format info
out <- list(projection )
names(out) <- c("projection")
out$format$type <- outFormat

# Change the GeoJSON format for successful task submission
onaq_js$features[[1]]$geometry$coordinates <- list(onaq_js$features[[1]]$geometry$coordinates)

task_info <- list(date, layers, out, onaq_js)                 # Create a list of data frames 
names(task_info) <- c("dates", "layers", "output", "geo")       # Assign names

task <- list(task_info, taskName, taskType)                     # Create a nested list 
names(task) <- c("params", "task_name", "task_type")            # Assign names  

toJSON function from jsonlite package converts the type of data frame to a string that can be recognized as a JSON object to be submitted as an area request.

task_json <- jsonlite::toJSON(task,auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 10)

title: 7  NASA’s Earth Observing System (EOS)
text:
7.34 Submit a Task Request
Token information is needed to submit a request. Below the login token is assigned to a variable.

token <- paste("Bearer", fromJSON(token_response)$token)     # Save login token to a variable

Below, post a call to the API task service, using the task_json created above.

# Post the point request to the API task service
response <- POST(paste0(API_URL, "task"), body = task_json , encode = "json", 
                 add_headers(Authorization = token, "Content-Type" = "application/json"))

task_content <- content(response)                           # Retrieve content of the request 
task_response <- toJSON(task_content, auto_unbox = TRUE)    # Convert the content to JSON and prettify it
prettify(task_response)                                     # Print the task response

A JSON downloaded from a previous request containing the information from that request can also be used if available

7.35 Retrieve Task Status
This API call will list all of the requests associated with your user account, automatically sorted by date, with the most recent requests listed first.
The AppEEARS API contains some helpful formatting resources. Below, limit the API response to 2 entries for the last 2 requests and set pretty to True to format the response as an organized JSON, making it easier to read. Additional information on AppEEARS API retrieve task, pagination, and formatting can be found in the API documentation.

params <- list(limit = 2, pretty = TRUE)                            # Set up query parameters
# Request the task status of last 2 requests from task URL
response_req <- GET(paste0(API_URL,"task"), query = params, add_headers(Authorization = token))
response_content <- content(response_req)                           # Retrieve content of the request
status_response <- toJSON(response_content, auto_unbox = TRUE)      # Convert the content to JSON object
remove(response_req, response_content)                              # Remove the variables that are not needed anymore     
prettify(status_response)                                           # Print the prettified response

text:
7.37 Download Files in a Request (Automation)
The bundle API provides information about completed tasks. For any completed task, a bundle can be queried to return the files contained as a part of the task request. Below, call the bundle API and return all of the output files. Next, read the contents of the bundle in JSON format and loop through file_id to automate downloading all of the output files into the output directory. For more information, please see AppEEARS API Documentation.

bundle <- fromJSON(bundle_response)$files
for (id in bundle$file_id){
  # retrieve the filename from the file_id
  filename <- bundle[bundle$file_id == id,]$file_name           
  # create a destination directory to store the file in
  filepath <- paste(outDir,filename, sep = "/")
  suppressWarnings(dir.create(dirname(filepath)))
  # write the file to disk using the destination directory and file name 
  response <- GET(paste0(API_URL, "bundle/", task_id, "/", id), 
                  write_disk(filepath, overwrite = TRUE), progress(),
                  add_headers(Authorization = token))
}

title: 8  USGS National Water Information System (NWIS)
text:
8.3 USGS Water Resources Mission:

Water information is fundamental to national and local economic well-being, protection of life and property, and effective management of the Nation’s water resources. The USGS works with partners to monitor, assess, conduct targeted research, and deliver information on a wide range of water resources and conditions including streamflow, groundwater, water quality, and water use and availability.

The United States Geological Survey (USGS) has collected water-resources data at approximately 1.5 million sites in all 50 States, the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, the Virgin Islands, Guam, American Samoa and the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands.









A map of collection sites can be found here

title: 8  USGS National Water Information System (NWIS)
text:
8.4 Types of USGS NWIS Data
The types of data collected are varied, but generally fit into the broad categories of surface water and groundwater.
Surface-water data, such as gage height (stage) and streamflow (discharge), are collected at major rivers, lakes, and reservoirs.
Groundwater data, such as water level, are collected at wells and springs.
Water-quality data are available for both surface water and groundwater. Examples of water-quality data collected are temperature, specific conductance, pH, nutrients, pesticides, and volatile organic compounds.
The NWIS web site serves current and historical data. Data are retrieved by category of data, such as surface water, groundwater, or water quality, and by geographic area.

section: 8.5 USGS R Packages: Collaborative and reproducible data analysis using R
text:
8.5 USGS R Packages: Collaborative and reproducible data analysis using R

Contributors: Jordan Read, Lindsay Carr Adapted from USGS ‘Getting Started with USGS R Packages’ course materials

Recently, the USGS has built a suite of software packages and tutorials for R users to interact with their data and streamline workflows. Here we have adapted course materials from their USGS R packages course materials written and developed by Lindsay R. Carr.
The common workflow for completing the data processing pipeline is subject to human error at every step: accessing data, analyzing data, and producing final figures. Multi-site analyses are especially error-prone because the same workflow needs to be repeated many times. This course teaches a modular approach to the common data analysis workflow by building on basic R data analysis skills and leveraging existing USGS R packages that can create advanced, reproducible workflows, such as for accessing gridded climate data, analyzing high frequency water observations, and for taking full advantage of the USGS ScienceBase repository. The USGS packages covered in this course span a variety of applications: accessing web data, accessing personally stored data, and releasing data for publication.
The modular workflows taught in this section will prepare researchers to create automated, robust data processing workflows through more efficient code development. Following the course, students will be capable of integrating these packages into their own scientific workflows.

8.5.1 Suggested prerequisite knowledge
This course assumes a moderate to advanced knowledge of the statistical programming language R. If you’re interested in using USGS packages for data analysis but have no R experience, please visit the Introduction to R curriculum available at this site.

Experience using R to import, view, and summarize data
Recommended: experience creating simple plots in R
Recommended: familiarity with RStudio



8.5.2 Course outline











Summary of Modules



Module
Description
Duration




dataRetrieval
Accessing time series data.
2 hours


geoknife
Accessing gridded data.
1 hour


Application
Use the packages introduced in previous modules to create and use a robust modular workflow.
1.5 hour







8.5.3 Software requirements
See the R installation instructions page for how to install/upgrade R and RStudio, add CRAN to your settings, and install some basic packages. Then, execute these lines so that you have the most up-to-date version of the packages used in this course.

install.packages('dataRetrieval')



8.5.4 Lesson Summary
This lesson will focus on finding and retrieving hydrologic time series data using the USGS R package, dataRetrieval. The package was created to make querying and downloading hydrologic data from the web easier, less error-prone, and reproducible. The package allows users to easily access data stored in the USGS National Water Information System (NWIS) and the multi-agency database, Water Quality Portal (WQP). NWIS only contains data collected by or for the USGS. Conversely, WQP is a database that aggregates water quality data from multiple agencies, including USGS, Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), US Department of Agriculture (USDA), and many state, tribal, and local agencies.
dataRetrieval functions take user-defined arguments and construct web service calls. The web service returns the data as XML (a standard data structure), and dataRetrieval takes care of parsing that into a usable R data.frame, complete with metadata. When web services change, dataRetrieval users aren’t affected because the package maintainers will update the functions to handle these modifications. This is what makes dataRetrieval so user-friendly.
Neither NWIS nor WQP are static databases. Users should be aware that data is constantly being added, so a query one week might return differing amounts of data from the next. For more information about NWIS, please visit waterdata.usgs.gov/nwis. For more information about WQP, visit their site www.waterqualitydata.us or read about WQP for aquatic research applications in the publication, Water quality data for national-scale aquatic research: The Water Quality Portal.


8.5.5 Lesson Objectives
Learn about data available in the National Water Information System (NWIS) and Water Quality Portal (WQP). Discover how to construct your retrieval calls to get exactly what you are looking for, and access information stored as metadata in the R object.
By the end of this lesson, the learner will be able to:

Investigate what data are available in National Water Information System (NWIS) and Water Quality Portal (WQP) through package functions.
Construct function calls to pull a variety of NWIS and WQP data.
Access metadata information from retrieval call output.



8.5.6 Lesson Resources

USGS publication: The dataRetrieval R package
Source code: dataRetrieval on GitHub
Report a bug or suggest a feature: dataRetrieval issues on GitHub
USGS Presentation: dataRetrieval Tutorial

title: 8  USGS National Water Information System (NWIS)
text:
8.6 Introduction to USGS R Packages
Before continuing with this lesson, you should make sure that the dataRetrieval package is installed and loaded. If you haven’t recently updated, you could reinstall the package by running install.packages('dataRetrieval') or go to the “Update” button in the “Packages” tab in RStudio.

# load the dataRetrival package
library(dataRetrieval)

The dataRetrieval package has undergone significant changes as legacy functions have been updated. Continued maintenance and changes to the package can be monitored at the dataRetrieval Status page.
There is an overwhelming amount of data and information stored in the National Water Information System (NWIS). This lesson will attempt to give an overview of what you can access. If you need more detail on a subject or have a question that is not answered here, please visit the NWIS help system.
crumbs: 8  USGS National Water Information System (NWIS)

title: 8  USGS National Water Information System (NWIS)
text:
8.7 Data available
Data types: NWIS and WQP store a lot of water information. NWIS contains streamflow, peak flow, rating curves, groundwater, and water quality data. As can be assumed from the name, WQP only contains water quality data.
Time series types: the databases store water data at various reporting frequencies, and have different language to describe these. There are 3 main types: unit value, daily value, and discrete. WQP only contains discrete data.

instantaneous value (sometimes called unit value) data is reported at the frequency in which it was collected, and includes real-time data. It is generally available from 2007-present.
daily value data aggregated to a daily statistic (e.g. mean daily, minimum daily, or maximum daily). This is available for streamflow, groundwater levels, and water quality sensors.
discrete data collected at a specific point in time, and is not a continuous time series. This includes most water quality data, groundwater levels, rating curves, surface water measurements, and peak flow.

Metadata types: both NWIS and WQP contain metadata describing the site at which the data was collected (e.g. latitude, longitude, elevation, etc), and include information about the type of data being used (e.g. units, dissolved or not, collection method, etc).
crumbs: 8  USGS National Water Information System (NWIS)

title: 8  USGS National Water Information System (NWIS)
text:
8.8 Common NWIS function arguments
monitoring_location_id All USGS water data are associated with geographic locations where measurements are collected. These are known as monitoring locations and include streamgages, groundwater wells, lakes, and other sites where water quantity and quality parameters are measured. Monitoring locations are identified using unique codes, typically an 8-digit identifier for surface-water sites or a 15-digit identifier for groundwater sites. In the new dataRetrieval functions, these are referred to as monitoring_location_id. Monitoring location identifiers include an agency prefix, such as "USGS-05427948". Always treat monitoring location identifiers as character strings rather than numeric values to prevent leading zeros from being dropped.
parameter_code USGS uses 5-digit codes to refer to specific measurements or constituents of interest, called parameter codes (parameter_code in dataRetrieval). For example, the code "00060" specifies discharge data. If you’d like to explore the full list, see the USGS Parameter Codes documentation. The package also provides a built-in parameter code table that you can access using read_waterdata_parameter_codes().
statistic_id When retrieving daily values, statistic_id specifies the statistical summary associated with a measurement. For example, "00001" represents the maximum, "00002" the minimum, and "00003" the mean. Daily values are identified using both a parameter code and a statistic identifier. Continuous measurements generally do not require this argument.
time Many of the new data retrieval functions use the time argument to specify the beginning and ending dates of a requested dataset. The argument accepts a character vector containing two dates in the format "YYYY-MM-DD". For example, time = c("2023-10-01", "2024-09-30"). Some functions instead use separate start_date and end_date arguments, so consult the documentation for the specific function being used.
state_name When querying monitoring location information, state_name specifies the U.S. state associated with the monitoring locations being requested. State names are provided as character strings (e.g., "Arizona" or "Wisconsin"). Additional filtering options are available, including site type, county, and other monitoring location characteristics.
For more query parameters and examples, visit the USGS Water Data API documentation and the dataRetrieval package documentation.
crumbs: 8  USGS National Water Information System (NWIS)

title: 8  USGS National Water Information System (NWIS)
text:
8.9 Discovering NWIS data
In some cases, users might have specific sites and data that they are pulling with dataRetrieval but what if you wanted to know what data exists in the database before trying to download it? You can use the function whatNWISdata, described below. Another option is to download the data using readNWISdata, and see the first and last available dates of that data with the arguments seriesCatalogOutput=TRUE and service="site". Downloading data will be covered in the next section, readNWIS.

8.9.1 whatNWISdata
whatNWISdata will return a data.frame specifying the types of data available for a specified major filter that fits your querying criteria. You can add queries by the data service, USGS parameter code, or statistics code. You need at least one “major filter” in order for the query to work. “Major filters” include siteNumber, stateCd, huc, bBox, or countyCd.
In this example, let’s find South Carolina stream temperature data. We specify the state, South Carolina, using the stateCd argument and South Carolina’s two letter abbreviation, SC.

data_sc <- whatNWISdata(stateCd="SC")
nrow(data_sc)

[1] 205353


Let’s look at the dataframe returned from whatNWISdata:

head(data_sc)

  agency_cd  site_no                station_nm site_tp_cd dec_lat_va

2      USGS 02110400 BUCK CREEK NEAR LONGS, SC         ST   33.95346

5      USGS 02110400 BUCK CREEK NEAR LONGS, SC         ST   33.95346
6      USGS 02110400 BUCK CREEK NEAR LONGS, SC         ST   33.95346
  dec_long_va coord_acy_cd dec_coord_datum_cd alt_va alt_acy_va alt_datum_cd
1   -78.71975            S              NAD83    5.3          0       NAVD88
2   -78.71975            S              NAD83    5.3          0       NAVD88
3   -78.71975            S              NAD83    5.3          0       NAVD88

1 03040206           ad    <NA>    <NA>      0       <NA>           wat
2 03040206           dv   00010   00001 124327       <NA>           wat

1        <NA>       0         0 2006-01-01 2025-01-01       20

The data returned from this query can give you information about the data available for each site including, date of first and last record (begin_date, end_date), number of records (count_nu), site altitude (alt_va), corresponding hydrologic unit code (huc_cd), and parameter units (parameter_units). These columns allow even more specification of data requirements before actually downloading the data. This function returns one row per unique combination of site number, dates, parameter, etc. In order to just get the sites, use unique:

sites_sc <- unique(data_sc$site_no)
length(sites_sc)

[1] 10216


To be more specific, let’s say we only want stream sites. This requires the siteType argument and the abbreviation “ST” for stream. See other siteTypes here. We also only want to use sites that have temperature data (USGS parameter code is 00010). Use the argument parameterCd and enter the code as a character string, otherwise leading zeroes will be dropped. Recall that you can see a table of all parameter codes by executing parameterCdFile in your console.

data_sc_stream_temp <- whatNWISdata(stateCd="SC", siteType="ST", parameterCd="00010")
nrow(data_sc_stream_temp)

[1] 768


We are now down to just 768 rows of data, much less than our original 205,353 rows. Downloading NWIS data will be covered in the next section, readNWIS.
The whatNWISdata function can also be very useful for making quick maps with site locations, see the columns dec_lat_va and dec_long_va (decimal latitude and longitude value). For instance,

# SC stream temperature sites
library(maps)
map('state', regions='south carolina')
title(main="South Carolina Stream Temp Sites")
points(x=data_sc_stream_temp$dec_long_va, 
       y=data_sc_stream_temp$dec_lat_va)




Geographic locations of NWIS South Carolina stream sites with temperature data




Continuing with the South Carolina temperature data example, let’s look for the mean daily stream temperature.

# Average daily SC stream temperature data
data_sc_stream_temp_avg <- whatNWISdata(
  stateCd="SC", 
  siteType="ST",
  parameterCd="00010",
  service="dv",
  statCd="00003")
nrow(data_sc_stream_temp_avg)

[1] 117


Let’s apply an additional filter to these data using the filter function from dplyr. Imagine that the trend analysis you are conducting requires a minimum of 300 records and the most recent data needs to be no earlier than 1975.

# Useable average daily SC stream temperature data
library(dplyr)
data_sc_stream_temp_avg_applicable <- data_sc_stream_temp_avg %>% 
  filter(count_nu >= 300, end_date >= "1975-01-01")
nrow(data_sc_stream_temp_avg_applicable)

[1] 117


This means you would have 117 sites to work with for your study.

title: 8  USGS National Water Information System (NWIS)
text:
8.10 Common WQP function arguments
countrycode, statecode, and countycode These geopolitical filters can be specified by a two letter abbreviation, state name, or Federal Information Processing Standard (FIPS) code. If you are using the FIPS code for a state or county, it must be preceded by the FIPS code of the larger geopolitical filter. For example, the FIPS code for the United States is US, and the FIPS code for South Carolina is 45. When querying with the statecode, you can enter statecode="US:45". The same rule extends to county FIPS; for example, you can use countycode="45:001" to query Abbeville County, South Carolina. You can find all state and county codes and abbreviations by executing stateCd or countyCd in your console.
siteType Specify the hydrologic location the sample was taken, e.g. streams, lakes, groundwater sources. These should be listed as a string. Available types can be found here.
organization The ID of the reporting organization. All USGS science centers are written “USGS-” and then the two-letter state abbreviation. For example, the Wisconsin Water Science Center would be written “USGS-WI”. For all available organization IDs, please see this list of org ids. The id is listed in the “value” field, but they are accompanied by the organization name in the “desc” (description) field. siteid This is the unique identification number associated with a data collection station. Site IDs for the same location may differ depending on the reporting organization. The site ID string is written as the agency code then the site number separated by a hyphen. For example, the USGS site 01594440 would be written as “USGS-01594440”.
characteristicName and characteristicType Unlike NWIS, WQP does not have codes for each parameter. Instead, you need to search based on the name of the water quality constituent (referred to as characteristicName in dataRetrieval) or a group of parameters (characteristicType in dataRetrieval). For example, “Nitrate” is a characteristicName and “Nutrient” is the characteristicType that it fits into. For a complete list of water quality types and names, see characteristicType list and characteristicName list.
startDate and endDate Arguments specifying the beginning and ending of the period of record you are interested in. For the dataRetrieval functions, these can be a date or character class in the form YYYY-MM-DD. For example, startDate = as.Date("2010-01-01") or startDate = "2010-01-01" could both be your input arguments.
crumbs: 8  USGS National Water Information System (NWIS)

title: 8  USGS National Water Information System (NWIS)
text:
8.11 Discovering WQP data
WQP has millions of records, and if you aren’t careful, your query could take hours because of the amount of data that met your criteria. To avoid this, you can query just for the number of records and number of sites that meet your criteria using the argument querySummary=TRUE in the function, readWQPdata. See the lesson on downloading WQP data to learn more about getting data. You can also use whatWQPsites to get the site information that matches your criteria.
Let’s follow a similar pattern to NWIS data discovery sections and explore available stream temperature data in South Carolina.

8.11.1 readWQPdata + querySummary
readWQPdata is the function used to actually download WQP data. In this application, we are just querying for a count of sites and results that match our criteria. Since WQP expects state and county codes as their FIPS code, you will need to use the string “US:45” for South Carolina.

wqpcounts_sc <- readWQPdata(statecode="US:45", querySummary = TRUE)
names(wqpcounts_sc)

 [1] "Date"                  "Content-Type"          "Connection"           
 [4] "Vary"                  "Vary-1"                "Vary-2"               
 [7] "Content-disposition"   "Total-Site-Count"      "NWIS-Site-Count"      
[10] "STORET-Site-Count"     "Total-Activity-Count"  "NWIS-Activity-Count"  
[13] "STORET-Activity-Count" "Total-Result-Count"    "NWIS-Result-Count"    
[16] "STORET-Result-Count"  


This returns a list with 16 different items, including total number of sites, breakdown of the number of sites by source (BioData, NWIS, STORET), total number of records, and breakdown of records count by source. Let’s just look at total number of sites and total number of records.

wqpcounts_sc[['Total-Site-Count']]

[1] "8220"

wqpcounts_sc[['Total-Result-Count']]

[1] "4447071"


This doesn’t provide any information about the sites, just the total number. I know that with 4,447,071 results, I will want to add more criteria before trying to download. Let’s continue to add query parameters before moving to whatWQPsites.

# specify that you only want data from streams
wqpcounts_sc_stream <- readWQPdata(statecode="US:45", siteType="Stream",
                                  querySummary = TRUE)
wqpcounts_sc_stream[['Total-Site-Count']]

[1] "2439"

wqpcounts_sc_stream[['Total-Result-Count']]

[1] "2225778"


2,225,778 results are still a lot to download. Let’s add more levels of criteria:

# specify that you want water temperature data and it should be from 1975 or later
wqpcounts_sc_stream_temp <- readWQPdata(statecode="US:45", siteType="Stream",
                                       characteristicName="Temperature, water",
                                       startDate="1975-01-01",
                                       querySummary = TRUE)
wqpcounts_sc_stream_temp[['Total-Site-Count']]

[1] "1858"

wqpcounts_sc_stream_temp[['Total-Result-Count']]

[1] "163220"


163,220 is little more manageable. We can also easily compare available stream temperature and lake temperature data.

wqpcounts_sc_lake_temp <- readWQPdata(statecode="US:45", 
                                      siteType="Lake, Reservoir, Impoundment",
                                      characteristicName="Temperature, water",
                                      startDate="1975-01-01",
                                      querySummary = TRUE)
# comparing site counts
wqpcounts_sc_stream_temp[['Total-Site-Count']]

[1] "1858"

wqpcounts_sc_lake_temp[['Total-Site-Count']]

[1] "877"

# comparing result counts
wqpcounts_sc_stream_temp[['Total-Result-Count']]

[1] "163220"

wqpcounts_sc_lake_temp[['Total-Result-Count']]

[1] "68215"


From these query results, it looks like South Carolina has much more stream data than it does lake data.
Now, let’s try our South Carolina stream temperature query with whatWQPsites and see if we can narrow the results at all.


8.11.2 whatWQPsites
whatWQPsites gives back site information that matches your search criteria. You can use any of the regular WQP web service arguments here. We are going to use whatWQPsites with the final criteria of the last query summary call - state, site type, parameter, and the earliest start date. This should return the same amount of sites as the last readWQPdata query did, .

# Getting the number of sites and results for stream 
# temperature measurements in South Carolina after 1975.
wqpsites_sc_stream_temp <- whatWQPsites(statecode="US:45", siteType="Stream",
                                       characteristicName="Temperature, water",
                                       startDate="1975-01-01")

Similar to what we did with the NWIS functions, we can filter the sites further using the available metadata in wqpsites_sc_stream_temp. We are going to imagine that for our study the sites must have an associated drainage area and cannot be below sea level. Using dplyr::filter:

# Filtering the number of sites and results for stream temperature 
# measurements in South Carolina after 1975 to also have an
# associated drainage area and collected above sea level.
wqpsites_sc_stream_temp_applicable <- wqpsites_sc_stream_temp %>% 
  filter(!is.na(DrainageAreaMeasure.MeasureValue),
         VerticalMeasure.MeasureValue > 0)

nrow(wqpsites_sc_stream_temp_applicable)

[1] 74


This brings the count down to a much more manageable 74 sites. Now we are ready to download this data.

8.12 readNWIS functions
We have learned how to discover data available in NWIS, but now we will look at how to retrieve data. There are many functions to do this, see the table below for a description of each. Each variation of readNWIS is accessing a different web service. For a definition and more information on each of these services, please see https://waterservices.usgs.gov/rest/. Also, refer to the previous lesson for a description of the major arguments to readNWIS functions.

text:
8.13 USGS Water Data retrieval functions
We have learned how to discover data available through USGS water data services, but now we will look at how to retrieve these data. The dataRetrieval package provides several functions for accessing different types of USGS water data through the new USGS Water Data APIs. Each function accesses a particular data service, such as daily values, continuous measurements, field measurements, or monitoring location metadata. The table below summarizes the primary functions available in dataRetrieval.
For additional information about each function and the services they access, see the USGS Water Data API documentation and the dataRetrieval function documentation.








Function
Description
Common arguments




read_waterdata()
Generalized USGS Water Data API retrieval function.
service, CQL, …, convertType, limit


read_waterdata_daily()
Returns USGS daily water data, such as mean daily discharge.
monitoring_location_id, parameter_code, statistic_id, time, approval_status, unit_of_measure, qualifier


read_waterdata_continuous()
Returns continuous USGS water data, such as instantaneous discharge and water temperature measurements.
monitoring_location_id, parameter_code, time, approval_status, unit_of_measure, qualifier, method_category


read_waterdata_field_measurements()
Returns discrete USGS field measurements, including groundwater and surface-water measurements.
monitoring_location_id, parameter_code, time, field_visit_id, observing_procedure_code, unit_of_measure


read_waterdata_channel()
Returns USGS channel measurement data associated with field visits.
monitoring_location_id, field_visit_id, measurement_number, channel_name, channel_flow, channel_width


read_waterdata_samples()
Returns USGS discrete water-quality sample data.
monitoringLocationIdentifier, characteristicGroup, characteristic, activityStartDateLower, activityStartDateUpper, dataProfile


read_waterdata_parameter_codes()
Returns USGS parameter code information.
parameter_code, parameter_name, unit_of_measure, parameter_group_code


read_waterdata_monitoring_location()
Returns information and metadata about USGS monitoring locations.
monitoring_location_id, agency_code, state_name, county_name, site_type, hydrologic_unit_code


read_waterdata_ts_meta()
Returns metadata describing available USGS time series at monitoring locations.
monitoring_location_id, parameter_code, statistic_id


read_waterdata_field_meta()
Returns metadata describing available USGS field measurements.
monitoring_location_id, parameter_code


read_waterdata_combined_meta()
Combines available metadata for multiple types of USGS water data.
monitoring_location_id


read_waterdata_stats_por()
Returns USGS daily statistics for the period of record.
monitoring_location_id, parameter_code, statistic_id, start_date, end_date


read_waterdata_stats_daterange()
Returns USGS daily statistics for a specified date range.
monitoring_location_id, parameter_code, statistic_id, start_date, end_date


read_waterdata_latest_daily()
Returns the latest available USGS daily values.
monitoring_location_id, parameter_code, statistic_id


read_waterdata_latest_continuous()
Returns the latest available USGS continuous measurements.
monitoring_location_id, parameter_code



The new Water Data API functions replace many of the legacy readNWIS functions. Unlike the previous approach, where individual functions were organized around NWIS web services, the new functions provide more specific access to different types of water data. Most functions accept a monitoring location identifier (monitoring_location_id) and additional filters such as parameter codes, statistic identifiers, and date ranges.
The generalized read_waterdata() function provides additional flexibility for constructing more complex queries. The service-specific functions provide a more straightforward approach when the type of data being retrieved is already known.
To discover what data are available at a particular monitoring location, use read_waterdata_combined_meta(), read_waterdata_ts_meta(), or read_waterdata_field_meta(). These functions return metadata describing the available data types, parameters, and periods of record.
The new Water Data APIs also support additional query filters, including state, county, site type, and geographic bounding boxes. For more information about available query parameters, consult the USGS Water Data API documentation.
The following are examples of how to use the different families of read_waterdata functions. Don’t forget to load the dataRetrieval library if you are in a new session.

read_waterdata_monitoring_location: Discover monitoring locations.
read_waterdata_combined_meta: Explore data availability at a monitoring location.
read_waterdata_daily: Retrieve daily discharge measurements.
read_waterdata_continuous: Retrieve continuous discharge measurements.
read_waterdata_field_measurements: Retrieve discrete field measurements.
read_waterdata_channel: Retrieve channel measurement data.
read_waterdata_parameter_codes: Explore USGS parameter codes.
read_waterdata_samples: Retrieve discrete water-quality samples.
read_waterdata_stats_por: Retrieve daily statistics for the period of record.
read_waterdata_latest_daily: Retrieve the latest available daily measurements.
read_waterdata_latest_continuous: Retrieve the latest available continuous measurements.

Each service-specific function is a wrapper for the more flexible readNWISdata. They set a default for the service argument and have limited user defined arguments. All readNWIS functions require a “major filter” as an argument, but readNWISdata can accept any major filter while others are limited to site numbers or state/county codes (see Table 1 for more info).
Other major filters that can be used in readNWISdata include hydrologic unit codes (huc) and bounding boxes (bBox). More information about major filters can be found in the NWIS web services documentation.
The following are examples of how to use each of the readNWIS family of functions. Don’t forget to load the dataRetrieval library if you are in a new session.

readNWISdata, county major filter
readNWISdata, huc major filter
readNWISdata, bbox major filter
readNWISdv
readNWISgwl
readNWISmeas
readNWISpCode
readNWISpeak
readNWISqw, multiple sites
readNWISqw, multiple parameters
readNWISrating, using base table
readNWISrating, corrected table
readNWISrating, shift table
readNWISsite
readNWISstat
readNWISuse
readNWISuv


8.13.1 read_waterdata
This function is the generalized retrieval function for accessing data through the new USGS Water Data APIs. It provides flexibility for constructing queries using different services and query parameters. Unlike the more specialized functions, read_waterdata() allows users to specify the service and additional query filters directly. For most common retrieval tasks, however, it is easier to use one of the service-specific functions, such as read_waterdata_daily() or read_waterdata_continuous(). See ?read_waterdata for more information.

Historic mean daily streamflow for sites in Maui County, Hawaii.
To retrieve daily streamflow measurements for multiple sites in a county, we first need to identify the monitoring locations within that county. We can use read_waterdata_monitoring_location() to discover these sites and then pass their monitoring location identifiers to read_waterdata_daily().

# Major filter: Maui County
# Service: daily values
# Parameter code: streamflow in cfs, 00060

MauiCo_avgdailyQ <- read_waterdata_daily(
    county_name = "Maui County",
    state_name = "Hawaii",
    parameter_code = "00060",
    statistic_id = "00003",
    time = c("2021-01-01", "2026-01-01"),
    skipGeometry = TRUE
)

head(MauiCo_avgdailyQ)

Historic minimum water temperatures for the HUC8 corresponding to the island of Maui, Hawaii. Hydrologic Unit Codes (HUCs) identify geographic areas that drain to a particular portion of the stream network. To retrieve data for a particular watershed, we can first identify monitoring locations within the HUC8 using read_waterdata_monitoring_location(). For a list of available HUCs, visit the USGS Watershed Boundary Dataset.
To see all HUCs available, visit https://water.usgs.gov/GIS/huc_name.html. The default statistic for daily values in readNWISdata is to return the max (00001), min (00002), and mean (00003). We will specify the minimum only for this example. You will need to use the statistic code, not the name. For all the available statistic codes, see the statType web service documentation and NWIS table mapping statistic names to codes. Caution! In readNWISdata and readNWISdv the argument is called statCd, but in readNWISstat the argument is statType.

# Specify the HUC8 corresponding to Maui
maui_huc8 <- "20020000"

# Discover stream monitoring locations within the HUC8
Maui_huc_sites <- read_waterdata_monitoring_location(
  hydrologic_unit_code = maui_huc8,
  site_type = "Stream",
  skipGeometry = TRUE
)

Requesting:
https://api.waterdata.usgs.gov/ogcapi/v1/collections/monitoring-locations/items?f=json&lang=en-US&site_type=Stream&hydrologic_unit_code=20020000&skipGeometry=TRUE&limit=50000

# How many locations were returned?
nrow(Maui_huc_sites)

[1] 693



Total nitrogen in mg/L for last 30 days around Great Salt Lake in Utah.
This example uses Sys.Date to get the most recent date, so your dates will differ. To get any data around Great Salt Lake, we will use a bounding box as the major filter. The bounding box must be a vector of decimal numbers indicating the western longitude, southern latitude, eastern longitude, and northern latitude. The vector must be in that order.

# Major filter: bounding box around Great Salt Lake 
# Service: water quality, qw
# Parameter code: total nitrogen in mg/L, 00600
# Beginning: this past 30 days, use Sys.Date()

prev30days <- Sys.Date() - 30

SaltLake_totalN <- read_waterdata_samples(
  boundingBox = c(-113.0428, 40.6474, -112.0265, 41.7018),
  activityStartDateLower = prev30days,
  activityStartDateUpper = Sys.Date()
)

# This service returns a lot of columns:
names(SaltLake_totalN)

# How many sites are returned?
length(unique(SaltLake_totalN$Location_Name))

8.13.8 readNWISrating
This function is the rating curve service function. It has a limited number of arguments and requires a site number. Follow along with the three examples below or see ?readNWISrating for more information.
There are three different types of rating tables that can be accessed using the argument type. They are base, corr (corrected), and exsa (shifts). For type=="base" (the default), the result is a data frame with 3 columns: INDEP, DEP, and STOR. For type=="corr", the resulting data frame will have 3 columns: INDEP, CORR, and CORRINDEP. For type=="exsa", the data frame will have 4 columns: INDEP, DEP, STOR, and SHIFT. See below for definitions of each column.

INDEP is the gage height in feet
DEP is the streamflow in cubic feet per second
STOR “*” indicates a fixed point of the rating curve, NA for non-fixed points
SHIFT indicates shifting in rating for the corresponding INDEP value
CORR are the corrected values of INDEP
CORRINDEP are the corrected values of CORR

There are also a number of attributes associated with the data.frame returned - url, queryTime, comment, siteInfo, and RATING. RATING will only be included when type is base. See this section for how to access attributes of dataRetrieval data frames.

Rating tables for Mississippi River at St. Louis, MO

# Major filter: site number, 07010000
# Type: default, base 

miss_rating_base <- read_waterdata_ratings(
  monitoring_location_id = "USGS-07010000"
)[[1]]

head(miss_rating_base$ratings)


# Major filter: site number, 07010000

miss_rating_corr <- read_waterdata_ratings(

  file_type = "corr"
)[[1]]

8.14 Additional Features

8.14.1 Accessing attributes
dataRetrieval returns a lot of useful information as “attributes” to the data returned. This includes site metadata information, the NWIS url used, date and time the query was performed, and more. First, you want to use attributes() to see what information is available. It returns a list of all the metadata information. Then you can use attr() to actually get that information. Let’s use the base rating table example from before to illustrate this. It has a special attribute called “RATING”.

# Major filter: site number, 07010000
# Type: default, base 
miss_rating_base <- readNWISrating(siteNumber="07010000")

# how many attributes are there and what are they?
length(attributes(miss_rating_base))
names(attributes(miss_rating_base))

# look at the site info
attr(miss_rating_base, "siteInfo")

# now look at the special RATING attribute
attr(miss_rating_base, "RATING")

All attributes are an R object once you extract them. They can be lists, data.frames, vectors, etc. If we want to use information from one of the attributes, index it just like you would any other object of that type. For example, we want the drainage area for this Mississippi site:

# save site info metadata as its own object
miss_site_info <- attr(miss_rating_base, "siteInfo")
class(miss_site_info)

# extract the drainage area
miss_site_info$drain_area_va



8.14.2 Using lists as input
readNWISdata allows users to give a list of named arguments as the input to the call. This is especially handy if you would like to build up a list of arguments and use it in multiple calls. This only works in readNWISdata, none of the other readNWIS... functions have this ability.

chicago_q_args <- list(siteNumbers=c("05537500", "05536358", "05531045"),
                       startDate="2015-10-01",
                       endDate="2015-12-31",
                       parameterCd="00060")

# query for unit value data with those arguments
chicago_q_uv <- readNWISdata(chicago_q_args, service="uv")
nrow(chicago_q_uv)

[1] 14488

# same query but for daily values
chicago_q_dv <- readNWISdata(chicago_q_args, service="dv")
nrow(chicago_q_dv)

[1] 151




8.14.3 Helper functions
There are currently 3 helper functions: renameNWIScolumns, addWaterYear, and zeroPad. renameNWIScolumns takes some of the default column names and makes them more human-readable (e.g. “X_00060_00000” becomes “Flow_Inst”). addWaterYear adds an additional column of integers indicating the water year. zeroPad is used to add leading zeros to any string that is missing them, and is not restricted to dataRetrieval output.
renameNWIScolumns
renameNWIScolumns can be used in two ways: it can be a standalone function following the dataRetrieval call or it can be piped (as long as magrittr or dplyr are loaded). Both examples are shown below. Note that renameNWIScolumns is intended for use with columns named using pcodes. It does not work with all possible data returned.

# get discharge and temperature data for July 2016 in Ft Worth, TX
ftworth_qt_july <- readNWISuv(siteNumbers="08048000", parameterCd=c("00060", "00010"), 
                              startDate="2016-07-01", endDate="2016-07-31")
names(ftworth_qt_july)

[1] "agency_cd"        "site_no"          "dateTime"         "X_00010_00000"   
[5] "X_00010_00000_cd" "X_00060_00000"    "X_00060_00000_cd" "tz_cd"           

# now rename columns
ftworth_qt_july_renamed <- renameNWISColumns(ftworth_qt_july)
names(ftworth_qt_july_renamed)

[1] "agency_cd"     "site_no"       "dateTime"      "Wtemp_Inst"   
[5] "Wtemp_Inst_cd" "Flow_Inst"     "Flow_Inst_cd"  "tz_cd"        


Now try with a pipe. Remember to load a package that uses %>%.

library(magrittr)

# get discharge and temperature data for July 2016 in Ft Worth, TX
# pipe straight into rename function
ftworth_qt_july_pipe <- readNWISuv(siteNumbers="08048000", parameterCd=c("00060", "00010"), 
                                   startDate="2016-07-01", endDate="2016-07-31") %>% 
  renameNWISColumns()

names(ftworth_qt_july_pipe)

[1] "agency_cd"     "site_no"       "dateTime"      "Wtemp_Inst"   
[5] "Wtemp_Inst_cd" "Flow_Inst"     "Flow_Inst_cd"  "tz_cd"        


addWaterYear
Similar to renameNWIScolumns, addWaterYear can be used as a standalone function or with a pipe. This function defines a water year as October 1 of the previous year to September 30 of the current year. Additionally, addWaterYear is limited to data.frames with date columns titled “dateTime”, “Date”, “ActivityStartDate”, and “ActivityEndDate”.

# mean daily discharge on the Colorado River in Grand Canyon National Park for fall of 2014
# The dates in Sept should be water year 2014, but the dates in Oct and Nov are water year 2015
co_river_q_fall <- read_waterdata_daily(
  monitoring_location_id = "USGS-09403850",
  parameter_code = "00060"
)

co_river_q_fall <- subset(
  co_river_q_fall,
  time >= as.Date("2018-09-28") &
  time <= as.Date("2018-11-30")
)

zeroPad
zeroPad is designed to work on any string, so it is not specific to dataRetrieval data.frame output like the previous helper functions. Oftentimes, when reading in Excel or other local data, leading zeros are dropped from site numbers. This function allows you to put them back in. x is the string you would like to pad, and padTo is the total number of characters the string should have. For instance if an 8-digit site number was read in as numeric, we could pad that by:

siteNum <- 02121500
class(siteNum)

class(siteNum_fix)

8.15 readWQP functions
After discovering Water Quality Portal (WQP) data in the data discovery section, we can now read it in using the desired parameters. There are two functions to do this in dataRetrieval. Table 1 describes them below.











Table 1. readWQP function definitions



Function
Description
Arguments




readWQPdata
Most general WQP data import function. Users must define each parameter.
..., service, querySummary, tz, ignore_attributes, convertType


readWQPqw
Used for querying by site numbers and parameter codes only.
siteNumbers, parameterCd, startDate, endDate, tz, legacy, querySummary, ignore_attributes, convertType





The main difference between these two functions is that readWQPdata is general and accepts any of the paremeters described in the WQP Web Services Guide. In contrast, readWQPqw has five arguments and users can only use this if they know the site number(s) and parameter code(s) for which they want data.
The following are examples of how to use each of the readWQP family of functions. Don’t forget to load the dataRetrieval library if you are in a new session.

readWQPdata, state, site type, and characteristic name
readWQPdata, county and characteristic group
readWQPdata, bbox, characteristic name, and start date
readWQPqw


8.15.1 readWQPdata
The generic function used to pull Water Quality Portal data. This function is very flexible. You can specify any of the parameters from the WQP Web Service Guide. To learn what the possible values for each, see the table of domain values. Follow along with the three examples below or see ?readWQPdata for more information.

# This takes about 3 minutes to complete.
WI_lake_phosphorus_2010 <- readWQPdata(statecode="WI",

Similar to the data frames returned from readNWIS functions, there are attributes (aka metadata) attached to the data. Use attributes to see all of them and attr to extract a particular attribute.

8.17 USGS Exercises Part 1

8.17.1 USGS Coding Lab









Recently NOAA published a press release demonstrating that 2020 was both the hottest and driest summer on record for Arizona. In this lab we will look at USGS NWIS stream gauge and precipitation data to investigate just how anomalous 2020 data are.
1: Use the readNWISstat function to retrieve the following statewide data for 2015-2020: 1. Precipitation total (inches/week) 2. Streamflow (ft^3/s)
2: Create two time series plots (one for preciptitation, one for streamflow), where color is a function of year (e.g. the x axis is month, the y axis is precipitation, legend shows color by year).

section: 9.2 The International Soil Moisture Network’s Mission and Design
text:
9.2 The International Soil Moisture Network’s Mission and Design
The International Soil Moisture Network is an infrastructure that compiles in situ soil data from across the globe into a centralized database. Data from dozens of different soil monitoring networks can be accessed on their website, and the data can be analyzed with their python package. It helps validate soil moisture data products from satellites, as well as being a database on its own. Along with soil moisture, the ISMN has expanded to have soil temperature and precipitation data among others, as well as information about soil properties in the metadata.
Founded at the TU Wien (Technical University of Wien), it now is operated by the Federal Institute of Hydrology (BfG) in Germany and the International Centre for Water Resources and Global Change (ICWRGC).


A map showing some of the networks in the ISMN. From the ISMN webpage.

title: 9  Introduction to the International Soil Moisture Network (ISMN) and Its Python Library
section: 9.3 Quality Assurance for Soil Moisture (QA4SM) Service
text:
9.3 Quality Assurance for Soil Moisture (QA4SM) Service
In addition to providing access to in situ soil moisture measurements, the ISMN is an important resource for validating satellite-derived soil moisture products. The Quality Assurance for Soil Moisture (QA4SM) service provides an interactive web-based platform for conducting these comparisons. Available at https://qa4sm.eu/, QA4SM allows users to evaluate satellite soil moisture products against ground-based observations from the ISMN, as well as reference datasets from land surface models and other sources. QA4SM also supports uploading custom datasets, allowing researchers to evaluate their own soil moisture products alongside the datasets already available within the platform. The service includes a public API, which will not be covered in this chapter.

section: 9.4 The Ecological Impacts of Soil Moisture
text:
9.4 The Ecological Impacts of Soil Moisture
Soil moisture refers to the water stored within the soil, particularly in its upper layers, and plays a fundamental role in ecosystem functioning. It influences vegetation growth, nutrient cycling, microbial activity, and the exchange of water and energy between terrestrial ecosystems and the atmosphere. Soil moisture is also an important variable for understanding and predicting droughts, floods, weather patterns, and greenhouse gas emissions.
Soil water availability helps sustain diverse microbial communities, which drive important biogeochemical processes and contribute to soil structure and nutrient availability. Conversely, prolonged or severe soil moisture deficits can lead to plant stress and mortality, reduce microbial activity and diversity, and disrupt soil processes. These changes can trigger reinforcing feedback loops that further degrade soil conditions and reduce ecosystem resilience.

title: 9  Introduction to the International Soil Moisture Network (ISMN) and Its Python Library
text:
9.5 Structure of the ISMN
The International Soil Moisture Network can be thought of as a “network of networks”, where thousands of local soil monitoring sites are compiled into one framework. Each country and network has their own way of recording data, which the ISMN accounts for in their harmonizing process. Some stations also measure additional features like precipitation and soil temperature along with moisture, which is also accessible in the same datasets.

9.5.1 Networks in the ISMN
The ISMN is made up of many different ecological research infrastructures across the country, which vary in scale. Some networks like SNOTEL (SNOwpackTELemetryNetwork) and SOILSCAPE in the United States are very large, each having 509 and 224 stations respectively. Smaller networks can have as few as just one sensor, like BFG_Nw in Germany.
Larger and more developed countries tend to have many networks within them, such as the United States, Germany the United Kingdom, and China. In other cases, networks can cross over international borders, such as the network ROMPS which has stations in Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, and Afghanistan.
A comprehensive list of all the networks in the ISMN can be found at: https://ismn.earth/en/networks/


9.5.2 Data Viewer and Web Portal
The ISMN Web Portal that contains most information from this chapter, as well as the data viewer and downloader. Here, there is metadata information about all the networks, visualizations of data, and information about the ISMN and their tools as a whole.
The web portal will be accessed later in this tutorial to download data. Also here is more information on the ISMN python package.


9.5.3 The ISMN’s Methodology
The ISMN contains surface and subsurface in-situ soil moisture data, collected across the globe. Since the data comes from different countries with different practices, it needs to be harmonized in terms of units. Then, advanced quality control is applied to the data, and it gets uploaded to the online database, with free public access. Quality flags that get used by the ISMN are explored later in this chapter. Additional metadata datasets are included for each station, which are the Köppen Geiger climate class, Harmonized World Soil Database, and ESA’s CCI landcover.


A depiction of how data is compiled from various sources into the ISMN database. Sourced from the ISMN website.



9.5.4 Metadata
Mandatory metadata information for each station comes from both the network operators as well as external data sources. For instance, soil properties, land cover and consistent climate are taken from external sources to provide consistency across all networks, and network operators can provide additional information on these. Network operators can also share quality control flags, which can all be accessed via the python tool (developed by TU Wien).
For each station in the database, soil moisture data is available from the surface down to deeper soil layers; the number of depths and the exact depths measured depend on the setup of the specific network. Along with soil moisture, stations can additionally measure soil temperature, air temperature, precipitation, soil suction, snow water equivalent, snow depth and surface temperature. These features are not available on all stations, but when so, they are accessible via the python tool.


Depiction of focus of ISMN data, a focus around soil moisture with additional features surrounding. Sourced from ISMN website

Networks are updated over ranges of times, some being daily, some monthly or every few months, and others at irregular intervals. It is preferred that data can be provided every hour, but that is not always the case. For historical data, there are usually only measurements once or twice a month, or even more irregular.


A graph showing frequency of readings per network. From the ISMN webpage.



9.5.5 Additional Metadata Datasets
As mentioned before, to get consistent metadata across networks, external data sources are used.
Harmonized World Soil Database (HWSD) - Used to retrieve soil information with 30’’ resolution (version v1.1).
CCI Landcover Classes - Land covers retrieved from ESA’s Climate Change Initiative, with 300m resolution (versions: 2000-v1.6.1, 2005-v1.6.1, 2010-v1.6.1).
Köppen-Geiger Climate Classes - Classifications of climates from the Köppen-Geiger database with an accuracy of 0.1 to 0.08 degrees respectively.
Soil and Landcover Information from Data Providers (not applicable to all networks) - When available, data providers and network operators may give their own measurements for climate, landcover etc. to go along with the data collected from previously mentioned sources.


9.5.6 How Soil Data is Collected
There are several techniques for measuring in situ soil moisture, the most commonly used are: frequency domain reflectance (FDR), time domain reflectometry (TDR) and capacitance, all measuring the dielectric properties of the soil, and cosmic-ray neutron sensors (CRNS). Regardless of the methods, they all result in volumetric soil moisture content, which can fit into the ISMN dataset.
Time Domain Reflectance (TDR) - Measures how fast electromagnetic pulses travel through soil, wetter soil slows them down. TDR is a very accurate method, and widely used in research. This is done by inserting metal rods horizontally at various depths in the soil then sends pulses down them, waiting for the return. The holes then get filled back in, and the sensors are usually then connected to a data logger which can regularly measure and record readings. The rods can also be inserted vertically at the surface(Rasheed 2022).
TDR systems do not need to account for any contents of the soil, nor do they need to be calibrated. This makes them very useful for spot measurements, without having to dig a hole and set up a sub-surface system(Rasheed 2022).


A TDR device in a hole about to be installed. Image courtesy of https://harvest.com/gallery/.

Frequency Domain Reflectometry (FDR) / Capacitance - Frequency domain reflectometry is very similar to TDR, except it uses an oscillating electric field rather than individual pulses. On top of that, FDR systems are cheaper, simpler, and requiere less power, making them popular for field use especially for long term temporal measurements(Rasheed 2022).
However, FDR systems are more sensitive to the contents of the soil, and can cause larger error if there is high salinity or mineral content(Rasheed 2022).


An FDR device out of the soil, courtesy of the Soil Moisture - FDR (Profile Probe) wikipedia page.

Cosmic-Ray Neutron Sensors (CRNS) - CRNS systems measure the amount of fast moving neutrons over a desired site. Soil moisture reduces the amount of fast moving neutrons. Mounted sensors above the ground measure the neutron flux over the site. A site can have a radius up to 240 meters, and a depth of up to 80 cm. A network that utilizes CRNS in the ISMN are the COSMOS networks, which are COSMOS (US) and COSMOS-UK, totaling 158 stations between them. To read more on CRNS and the COSMOS networks, see https://globalcosmos.github.io/.


A infographic showing ranges of multiple soil moisture detection systems, including stationary and mobile CRNS systems. Image courtesy of Global COSMOS.net (https://globalcosmos.github.io/).



9.5.7 Data Quality
The ISMN uses quality flags to mark “dubious” data. There are two categories of flags, C and D. C flags are automatically assigned when a reading passes a certain threshold, making it suspicious. D flags are used in more case-by-case events, like strange spikes, or peaking soil moisture without any precipitation events. Reference https://ismn.earth/en/data/flag-overview/ for more in-depth information on ISMN data flags.
When downloading data from the ISMN data viewer, there are options to filter out anything except “good” data, which isn’t flagged.


9.5.8 Harmonization
Since there are no standardizations across networks, the ISMN has to process all of it domestically. When it comes to measuring soil moisture, there are many definitions such as: volumetric, water depth, mass, Soil Moisture Index, and plant available water. On top of that, there are different installation depths and positions (horizontal and vertical) among many other things. Because of this, datasets are harmonized in time, and in measurement units.
All soil moisture data in the ISMN database are in (m3/m-3), which is the most commonly used unit. Other measurements get their own respective standards which they get harmonized to. For time, all measurements are converted to Coordinated Universal Time (UTC).
Measurements that fall outside of normal ranges get labeled with quality flags, and datasets are harmonized to an hourly timestep NaN values (Not a Number) or missing timesteps are possible).


An infographic depicting the process of harmonizing data for the ISMN. Courtesy the ISMN website.

text:
9.6 Downloading data from the ISMN Website
Website link: https://ismn.earth/en/
The first step of working with ISMN data is downloading from the website. To do so, you will need to create an account and sign in (it’s free).
From the home page, click on the “data access” button, and make sure that you are signed into your account. From there, you should be looking at the data viewer window with all available networks, something like this:


Image captured from ISMN data viewer/downloader.

On the left side, there are settings to select what networks will be included in the download, such as inputting coordinates, checking boxes, or drawing out areas on the map. There are also settings like including all climates, land covers etc. At the very bottom right of the window, it shows how many time series are being selected.


Image from ISMN tool manual.

For the tutorial later in the chapter, we will only be selecting a handful of sites from Europe, visible in the picture below. These sites are FMI, GTK, REMEDHUS, RSMN, SMOSMANIA, VAS and WEGENERNET. For the time range, we will be using January 1, 2009, to December 31, 2020. Be sure to check the All variables, all climates and all land covers on the “more options” page too. Then click the “Download” button, and the screen below should appear.


Image captured from ISMN data viewer/downloader.

On this page DO NOT check the gap filling with NaN box, and the other boxes do not matter too much, for this tutorial the quality flags being at least good is used. Once everything looks good, click Download. The process can take a few minutes to complete. In the bottom right corner, there is a “your requests” button which has the links of your requests, which you will need to download, which will take a few more minutes. Links to download can also be found in your account’s email, depending on the time taken to download. Once the .zip file is on your local machine, you are ready to begin coding. You do not need to unzip this folder and take note of its path.

9.7 Hands On Part 1: Intro to the ismn Python Library
Now, we will begin the hands on coding exercise in Python. In this segment, we will work with the data downloaded from the tutorial above to examine it’s structure and create graphs.

9.7.1 Python Requirements
Unlike other sections throughout the textbook, this section uses Python. If you have not used Python on your local machine before, you will first need to install it. Python can be downloaded from the official website (https://www.python.org/downloads/). Alternatively, you can install Python through the Anaconda distribution (https://www.anaconda.com/download), which provides Python along with tools for managing packages and computational environments.
python --version
For this tutorial, Python version 3.12 was used, along with Jupyter Notebook as the development environment (IDE). Jupyter Notebook provides an interactive environment where Python code can be executed in individual cells, making it particularly useful for data analysis and visualization.
To install Jupyter Notebook using pip, run the following command in your terminal:
pip install notebook
Once installed, you can launch Jupyter Notebook by running:
jupyter notebook
You are welcome to use another Python development environment, such as Visual Studio Code or JupyterLab, provided it supports running Python code. Regardless of which environment you choose, make sure it can access the .zip file downloaded from the ISMN website, as this file will be used throughout the tutorial.


9.7.2 Data Prepping
First, let’s import required packages. The main focus is the ISMN_Interface function, which comes from the ismn package. This can be downloaded using pip install ismn from the command line. In this tutorial, we will also be using the numpy and matplotlib packages which also need their own downloads using pip. Source code is from the ISMN’s coding tutotial located at: https://ismn.readthedocs.io/en/latest/examples/interface.html
from ismn.interface import ISMN_Interface
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # matplotlib is not installed automatically

ismn_data = ISMN_Interface(FILE_PATH)

10.1 Plotting Sensor Data
Now, let’s examine a sensor at the SaintFelixdeLauragais station. The available sensors to pick from are visible from sections before, here we chose the “ThetaProbe-ML2X_soil_moisture_0.050000_0.050000” sensor. After getting the sensor as an object, let’s turn it’s metadata into a PANDAS dataframe. Then, we will plot the sensor’s soil moisture data as a time series.
In the output, we see a the metadata for the sensor, as well as a simple time series of measurements from that specific sensor. That gap around 2011 in the time series could be caused from various reasons like dubious data or sensor malfunctions.
# print the sensor's metadata
sensor = ismn_data['SMOSMANIA']['SaintFelixdeLauragais']['ThetaProbe-ML2X_soil_moisture_0.050000_0.050000']

10.5 Plotting Station Locations
Here, we are plotting station locations on a map, only if their depth for ‘soil_moisture’ measurement are out of desired depth range. To do so, desired min and max depth are passed through the plot_station_locations function. Same can be done with the ‘soil_temperature’ variable.
import cartopy.crs as ccrs

ismn_data.plot_station_locations('soil_temperature', min_depth=0.5, ax=axs[1], markersize=5, text_scalefactor=3)

text:
11.1 Selecting and Reading Different Sensors based off Metadata
To select sensors with specific features, the get_dataset_ids function can be used. Passing through ‘soil_temperature’ as the variable, along with a ‘max_depth’ of 1m, as well as a ‘lc_2005’ (land cover 2005) of 130 and ‘climate_KG’ type of ‘Csb’, we get 4 stations that meet these criteria. The same result can be gotten using masking, done in the following cell.
# get sesnors with soil temp readings, a max depth of 1m, and specific land cover and climate values 
ids = ismn_data.get_dataset_ids(variable='soil_temperature',
                                max_depth=1,
                                filter_meta_dict={'lc_2005': 130, 'climate_KG': 'Csb'})
# look at the sensors that meet requirements
ids
[456, 458, 460, 462]
# alternate way to calling function above, another method of filtering sensors
conditions = (ismn_data.metadata['variable'].val == 'soil_temperature') & \
             (ismn_data.metadata['instrument'].depth_to <= 1) & \
             (ismn_data.metadata['lc_2005'].val == 130) & \
             (ismn_data.metadata['climate_KG'].val == 'Csb')

# apply the mask and look at the valid stations
ismn_data.metadata[conditions].index.to_list()
[456, 458, 460, 462]
Using the stations’ IDs that we just gathered from masking, we can plot a time series of soil temperature. Since not every station measures soil temperature, masking the data first is an important step to get soil temperature since it is not available at every station.
# plot the filtered sensor ids for soil temp
ts, meta = ismn_data.read(ids, return_meta=True)
ax = ts.plot(figsize=(12,4), title=f'Time series for ID {ids[1]}', xlabel="Time [year]", ylabel="Soil Temp. [°C]")

11.2 Selecting by Variable and Depth
Here, we will get lists of sensors that meet requirements. In the next block of code, only sensor with soil moisture readings from 0-0.05 meters are iterated through, and their information is shown and plotted. In this example, the ismn_data.collection.iter_sensors function returns networks, stations, and sensors that apply. (It returns a lot of text, so here we will stop after the first sensor)
# iterate through only stations that have soil moisture data at a depth from 0 to 0.05m 
for network, station, sensor in ismn_data.collection.iter_sensors(variable='soil_moisture',
                                                                  depth=[0., 0.05]):
    
    # print general information for sensors that match from each network
    display(network)
    display(station)
    display(sensor)

    # print the first sensor's metadata
    print('\033[1m' + f'Metadata for sensor {sensor}:'+ '\033[0m')
    display(sensor.metadata.to_pd())
    ax = sensor.data.plot(figsize=(12,4), title=f'Time series for sensor {sensor.name}')
    ax.set_xlabel("Time [year]")
    ax.set_ylabel("Soil Moisture [$m^3 m^{-3}$]")
    break  # for this example we stop after the first sensor

11.5 Selecting by Variables and Other Metadata
Now, in a similar process as before, we will iterate through sensors and their corresponding sensors that have data for precipitation measurements with ‘lc_2010’ values 10 (Cropland) or 130 (Grassland). The function iter_sensors will return the station and sensor values. Here, we will plot precipitation values.
# iterate through sensors and corresponding stations with precipitation readings with lc_2010 values 10 or 130
for station, sensor in ismn_data['RSMN'].iter_sensors(variable='precipitation',
                                                      filter_meta_dict={'lc_2010': [10, 130]}):
    # print station and sensor names
    display(station)
    display(sensor)

    # get the metadata from the sensor
    data = sensor.read_data()
    metadata = sensor.metadata

    # plot precip data for the first sensor in iteration
    print('\033[1m' + f'Metadata for sensor {sensor}:' + '\033[0m')
    display(metadata.to_pd())
    ax = data.plot(figsize=(12,4), title=f'Time series for sensor {sensor.name}')
    ax.set_xlabel("Time [year]")
    ax.set_ylabel("Precipitation [mm]")
    break # for this example we stop after the first sensor

Once again, we will filter through sensors, but this time for sensor depth between 0 and 0.05m, specific climates (refer to the Köppen Geiger table for exact definitions), and the same land cover values as before.
from ismn.meta import Depth
for network, station, sensor in ismn_data.collection \
    .iter_sensors(variable='soil_moisture',
                  depth=Depth(0.,0.05),
                  filter_meta_dict={'lc_2010': [10, 130],
                                    'climate_KG':['Csc', 'Cfa', 'Dfc']}):

    display(station)
    display(sensor)

    # set all non good data flagged values as NaN
    data = sensor.read_data()

    metadata = sensor.metadata

    # look at the sensor's metadata

    ax.set_ylabel("Soil Moisture [$m^3 m^{-3}$]")
    break # for this example we stop after the first sensor

11.7 Creating Subset Interface
The ISMN_Interface tool also has capabilities to make subsets of itself. Using the subset_from_ids function, we can do so. First, we randomly choose 10 sensor ids from sensors with soil moisture data, and put those sensors into the new subset.
# metadata from stations with soil moisture data
metadata = ismn_data.metadata[ismn_data.metadata[('variable', 'val')] == 'soil_moisture']

np.random.seed(123)
ids = np.random.choice(metadata.index, 10)

# create the subset of 10 random sensors, store in the subset object
subset = ismn_data.subset_from_ids(ids)

text:
10.2 GEE Overview:


The Google Earth Engine (GEE) platform combines a multi-petabyte catalog of satellite imagery and geospatial datasets with the massive computational power of Google’s cloud infrastructure. Rather than downloading and processing large datasets locally, GEE users can leverage Google’s distributed computing resources to perform complex analyses across large spatial and temporal scales. This architecture enables planetary-scale environmental monitoring and analysis that would otherwise require substantial local computing resources and data storage.
Scientists, researchers, and developers use Earth Engine to detect environmental changes, identify trends, and quantify processes occurring across the Earth’s surface. Students and academic researchers can access Earth Engine at no cost for eligible noncommercial educational and research activities. Commercial use is also supported through separate pricing arrangements.
