section: 10.5 Hands on: Using the GEE Code Editor
text:
10.5 Hands on: Using the GEE Code Editor
GEE makes their data available through a number of different channels and tools. This flexibility reflects the way geospatial data are handled in Earth Engine: rather than downloading datasets locally, users send computational requests to remote servers where the data are stored and processed. These requests are made through a set of APIs and client libraries that translate user-written code into Earth Engine operations.
Access to Earth Engine data is typically mediated through these client libraries, which provide interfaces in both JavaScript and Python. These libraries act as a bridge between user-written code and the Earth Engine servers, allowing complex geospatial analyses to be expressed in a relatively compact and high-level syntax. Users can also interact directly with Earth Engine through a REST API, although this is less commonly used for exploratory analysis.
One of the most widely used interfaces is the JavaScript-based Code Editor, which provides an interactive, browser-based environment for working with Earth Engine data. The Python client library offers similar functionality, and can be used in environments such as Google Colab, local Python installations, or cloud-based platforms such as App Engine. Together, these interfaces allow users to choose a workflow that best fits their computational background and research needs.

10.5.1 Setting Up an Earth Engine Account
Before accessing any of the interfaces described above, a Google Earth Engine account is required. As of 2024, registration is no longer a standalone process. Earth Engine access is granted at the level of a Google Cloud project, which is linked to your Google account. This change was made to support the platform’s commercial release while preserving free access for academic and research users.
To register:

Sign in at https://code.earthengine.google.com/register with the Google account you intend to use for Earth Engine (e.g., @nau.edu email).
Choose the noncommercial/academic use option when prompted.
Either select an existing Google Cloud project or create a new one. Most new users will create a project at this stage; the project name (e.g., ee-yourusername) which you will later pass to ee.Initialize() or ee_Initialize() from the Python and R client libraries.
Confirm registration. Approval is typically immediate for noncommercial use.

A note on quotas: in 2026, Earth Engine introduced a tiered quota system for noncommercial projects. Projects that have not selected a tier are placed in the Community Tier by default, which is sufficient for coursework and exploratory analysis but applies stricter rate limits than higher tiers. If you find that long-running scripts begin to fail with OverQuotaError, the quota tier of your project is the first thing to check. Tier selection is done from the Earth Engine project management page at https://code.earthengine.google.com/register.
Once registered, the Code Editor at https://code.earthengine.google.com/ is immediately accessible. No further authentication is required from the browser. The Python and R client libraries each require an additional local authentication step, which is described in the Other Interfaces section later in this chapter.


10.5.2 The GEE Code Editor
GEE provides access to a Code Editor as an integrated development environment (IDE) for the Earth Engine JavaScript API. This IDE offers a platform to write and execute code, visualize results on an interactive map, and manage scripts and projects within a single web-based environment. The Code Editor is accessed through a dedicated webpage:
https://code.earthengine.google.com/
Access to Earth Engine data through the Code Editor is built around the JavaScript programming language, which serves as the primary scripting interface for this environment. JavaScript provides a lightweight and accessible syntax that acts as a direct bridge to the Earth Engine API, where all geospatial computations are performed. Although JavaScript may not be the most familiar programming language for many researchers in the geosciences, it is the most mature and fully supported option within Earth Engine. Importantly, users do not need to become expert JavaScript programmers to use the platform effectively. Instead, a basic understanding of syntax is sufficient, since most operations in Earth Engine are performed by calling pre-built functions from the Earth Engine library. This brief introduction to JavaScript syntax for GEE provided by the GEE developer team is enough to get started for most use cases.
When first accessing the Code Editor, you may be prompted to create a home folder. This folder is permanently linked to your Earth Engine account and serves as your personal workspace within the platform. It is good practice to choose a name that clearly identifies you, since this will be visible within shared Earth Engine environments and collaborative workflows.
Within your home folder, you can organize and store scripts and repositories, which function similarly to projects and code files in other development environments.
The Code Editor interface is divided into four main panels:

Script Manager (left panel): Organizes your saved scripts and repositories
Script Editor (center panel): Where you write and edit JavaScript code
Console (top-right panel): Displays printed outputs, errors, and logs
Map Display (bottom panel): Visualizes geospatial data and analysis results










When learning a new programming environment, it is traditional to begin with a simple output such as “Hello World!”. In Earth Engine, we can adapt this to “Hello Earth!” to verify that the Code Editor is working and to become familiar with running scripts and viewing console output.
To do this, enter the following code in the Script Editor and execute the script by clicking Run at the top of the panel, or by pressing Ctrl + Enter:

print('Hello Earth!');

You should see the text output appear in the upper-right panel under “Console”. This is basic JavaScript, which runs in your web browser on the client side. The power of GEE is in taking advantage of Google’s vast infrastructure of servers to both access data and perform calculations on the server side. This client-server distinction is important in GEE and can be read about here. We can now begin using GEE to access data on the server side, specifically, images and image collections.


10.5.3 Working with Earth Engine Image Objects
Before writing any code, it is useful to understand that the Earth Engine API’s functionality is organized around objects (e.g., Earth Engine images, image collections, features, and feature collections) and associated methods, which are built-in functions that operate on these object types. Detailed documentation for these object types and their methods is provided in the ‘Docs’ panel on the upper left of the Code Editor. (See here for more information on GEE objects and methods).
Let’s now begin working with GEE objects by accessing an image from Landsat 8, one of the most widely used Earth Observation platforms. In the Script Editor, enter and run the following code:

var firstImage = ee.Image("LANDSAT/LC08/C02/T1_L2/LC08_037035_20250619");

Notice the syntax. A new variable is declared using var, and each statement is terminated with a semicolon (;). Up to this point, this follows basic JavaScript conventions. Next, we assign the variable a GEE Image object using ee.Image(), passing the satellite image ID as an argument. Once the variable is created, we can add it to the map using Map.addLayer().

Map.addLayer(firstImage);

Notice that Map is another GEE object type, and methods such as .addLayer() provide means to interact with the Map Display of the Code Editor.
The image should appear in your Map Display, however, we still need to adjust the image visualization parameters to make it visualize nicely. In this case, we can visualize the image using true color by entering the following parameters at the beginning of the script:

var trueColorVis = {              // a dictionary object 
  bands: ["SR_B4","SR_B3","SR_B2"], // Use the Red, Green, Blue bands
  min: 8000, // minimum pixel value range
  max: 18000}; // maximum pixel value range 

Then modify the Map.addLayer() statement to include the visualization parameters and a title for the image. The argument order is: (image object, visualization parameters, layer title).

Map.addLayer(firstImage, trueColorVis, "First Image");

You should now be able to see your first satellite image, visualized over Flagstaff, Arizona and the Grand Canyon.









With an image now loaded into the GEE development environment, we can inspect it in various ways. In the upper-right panel, click the Inspector tab. Then with your cursor, click on a pixel of the satellite image on the Map Display. You will see some information populate the Inspector panel.









In the Inspector panel, open the Objects section, and click on bands. We can see that this Landsat 8 image contains 19 bands. Under properties, we can see that the image also includes a lot of metadata, such as CLOUD_COVER, DATE_ACQUIRED, SUN_AZIMUTH, etc. These properties will be useful for filtering image collections in the future.


10.5.4 Working With Image Collections
We previously loaded one single Landsat image to the map. But the true power of GEE is in working with image collections, which can represent an entire catalogue of data from a specific satellite or database.
Let’s use Landsat 8 once again. We can type the ID of the satellite into an ee.ImageCollection() object, much as we did above. But this time we can search for this collection using the search bar. In the upper search bar at the top of the code editor webpage, type “Landsat 8” and click Enter. There will be several results representing different processing levels. Find the dataset titled USGS Landsat 8 Level 2, Collection 2, Tier 1.





Note: You can access any of the datasets in Google Earth Engine this way. The search bar is a way to explore GEE’s petabytes of Earth data!




This dataset contains already pre-processed atmospherically corrected surface reflectance data, which is what we want to work with. Click on this search result to inspect the details of this dataset. Inside, there is a Description, list of Bands, Properties, and Terms of Use. By clicking on the Bands tab, we can inspect which of the bands we saw earlier correspond to which sections of the electromagnetic spectrum (blue, green, red, near infrared, shortwave infrared, etc.). We can also see the spatial resolution of the data, which here is 30 meters2.
Scrolling down, we can see on the lefthand side the period of Dataset Availability (2013-03-18 to present), the Dataset Provider (USGS), and a Collection Snippet which we can use to programmatically bring the dataset into our script. Copy the collection snippet, close this window, and let’s paste the snippet into the script.









This code snippet creates a GEE image collection object, and we need only provide a variable name to contain it. In this case, we can assign this object the name landsat8. With one line of code, landsat8 now contains ALL data in the Landsat 8 catalogue, spanning 2013 to present and covering the entire globe!

var landsat8 = ee.ImageCollection("LANDSAT/LC08/C02/T1_L2");


10.5.4.1 Filtering an Image Collection
While having all of the data from Landsat 8 in one object is interesting, it’s not very useful. We need to filter the image collection to focus on the time and location of interest. We can filter spatially to focus on an area of interest, and temporally to narrow in on a particular timeframe.
To apply a spatial filter, we will create an Earth Engine Feature object. The Map Display allows one way to do this manually. On the map panel, click the Point icon, then click a point of interest where you would like to see satellite imagery on your map. I’ll choose southern California near Los Angeles.









Once a point is placed, notice that it is automatically converted to a Geometry Import. It will appear under Geometry Imports on the map, and will also appear as var geometry at the imports section above your scripting panel. The same feature could have been created programmatically as well, for example: var geometry = ee.Geometry.Point([-118.64,34.10]);.
This feature can now be used to filter the image collection to only include images which spatially intersect the created point. This is done by applying the method .filterBounds() to the Image Collection.

var landsat8 = ee.ImageCollection("LANDSAT/LC08/C02/T1_L2")
  .filterBounds(geometry);

With the Image Collection filtered spatially, the next step is to apply a temporal filter. To perform this, the method .filterDate() can be called and passed a date range as arguments. In this case the image collection will be filtered for dates in between 2024-11-01 and 2024-12-31.

var landsat8 = ee.ImageCollection("LANDSAT/LC08/C02/T1_L2")
  .filterBounds(geometry) //spatial filter
  .filterDate("2024-11-01", "2024-12-31"); // temporal filter 

Notice how each filter can build on the last. With the spatial and temporal filter applied, we can now add the collection to the map using the following command and including the image visualization parameters from above.

Map.addLayer(landsat8, trueColorVis, "Landsat 8 Collection");

An image collection consists of multiple independent image objects. To inspect them, click on the Inspector tab of the upper-right panel. Then click on the data on your map. In this case, we can see in the Inspector panel that there are four image objects in the image collection.












10.5.5 Dealing with Clouds
Take a look at your image collection on the map. You will likely only see the first image in the collection. Does it have any clouds?
Clouds are an ever-present challenge when working with satellite data. Even if your area of interest is clear in the topmost image, there’s no guarantee it’s unobstructed in the other images of the collection. To handle this, we’ll explore three methods:

Median compositing: Calculate the median pixel value across the collection. This often removes bright pixels caused by clouds, especially when there is a lot of data.
Filtering by attributes: Remove images with high cloud cover using the metadata property.
Cloud masking: Apply a mask that identifies and removes clouds at the pixel level.


10.5.5.1 Median Compositing
The simplest way to reduce clouds in an image collection is to apply a mathematical operation across the entire collection. While this may sound complex, Earth Engine makes it straightforward.
Each band in an image can be thought of as a 2D array of pixel values, which allows mathematical operations to be applied across images. For an image collection, the .median() method reduces the collection to a single image by computing the median value at each pixel location.
Because clouds tend to have high reflectance in optical imagery, they often appear as unusually bright values within a time series. By taking the median at each pixel, these outliers are suppressed, resulting in a composite image close to the true median surface reflectance values–particularly when there are many cloud-free images.
Implement this by creating a new object called landsat8_median:

var landsat8_median = ee.ImageCollection("LANDSAT/LC08/C02/T1_L2")
  .filterBounds(geometry)
  .filterDate("2024-11-01", "2024-12-31")
  .median();

The result of this operation is no longer an image collection, but a single image object. In GEE parlance, moving from a collection to a single image is referred to as reducing the image collection.
Visualize the resulting image using the same visualization parameters as above. Did the clouds disappear?









In this case, not entirely. This is due to the fact that there were only four images in the collection. However, in a sunny region like California, compositing across a longer time span would result in a much sharper image. What would it look like had we collapsed a year of data using this method?
This approach is quick and effective for producing a general visual overview, but it can introduce distortions and results in the loss of potentially valuable temporal information. To handle clouds more precisely while preserving information through time, we can explore alternative methods.


10.5.5.2 Filtering by Image Properties
Recall that each image includes a set of properties, which are metadata associated with the scene. Landsat data include the property CLOUD_COVER, which represents the estimated percentage of cloud cover for a given image. For example, if an image’s property CLOUD_COVER = 40, then approximately 40% of the scene is estimated to be obscured by clouds based on USGS processing algorithms.
We can use this property to filter out images that are too cloudy for analysis. To do so, we append an additional filter step to the image collection:

var landsat8 = ee.ImageCollection('LANDSAT/LC08/C02/T1_L2')
  .filterBounds(geometry)
  .filterDate('2024-11-01', '2024-12-31')
  .filter(ee.Filter.lt('CLOUD_COVER', 20));

Here, we use the .filter() method to apply an additional condition to the image collection. The condition is defined using ee.Filter.lt(), which selects images where a specified property is less than a given threshold. In this case, we use the CLOUD_COVER property to retain only images with less than 20% estimated cloud cover.
The resulting image collection contains only images that meet this condition, in addition to the spatial and temporal filters applied earlier. A cloud cover threshold of 20% may be sufficient for relatively cloud-free regions such as southern California, but the threshold can be adjusted depending on local climate conditions, data availability, and analysis objectives.


10.5.5.3 Cloud Masking
A more robust way to handle clouds is by applying a cloud mask. Unlike simple filtering, which removes entire images, cloud masking operates at the pixel level, allowing us to retain useful observations within partially cloudy scenes.
To implement this approach, we first define a cloud masking function. This introduces an important Earth Engine concept: applying a function across all images in a collection using the .map() method.
For widely used sensors such as Landsat and Sentinel, well-tested cloud masking functions are readily available in the Earth Engine community and documentation. Here, we use a standard Landsat approach that leverages the QA_PIXEL band to identify clouds and cloud shadows based on quality assessment flags. For more information on the Landsat Quality Assessment (QA) bands and the bit flags used to identify clouds, cloud shadows, and other atmospheric conditions, see the USGS Documentation.
To implement this, we first define the masking function. Add the following code at the top of your script:

function maskL8sr(image) { // intake an image
  var qa = image.select('QA_PIXEL'); // select the QA pixel band

  // define the cloud mask using Landsat 8's included bitmap codes in the QA band  
  var cloudMask = qa.bitwiseAnd(1 << 1).eq(0) // Dilated cloud
    .and(qa.bitwiseAnd(1 << 2).eq(0))         // Cirrus
    .and(qa.bitwiseAnd(1 << 3).eq(0))         // Cloud
    .and(qa.bitwiseAnd(1 << 4).eq(0));        // Cloud shadow

  return image.updateMask(cloudMask); // return the masked image 
}

Now that we have defined a cloud masking function, we can apply it to every image in the collection. In GEE, this is known as mapping a function over an image collection.
This is done using the .map() method, which applies a function to each image in the collection and returns a new, processed collection as output. The following code applies both the cloudiness attribute filter and the cloud masking function to every image in the collection, resulting in a more robust approach to dealing with cloud cover.

var landsat8 = ee.ImageCollection('LANDSAT/LC08/C02/T1_L2')
  .filterBounds(geometry)
  .filterDate('2024-11-01', '2024-12-31')
  .filter(ee.Filter.lt('CLOUD_COVER', 20)) 
  .map(maskL8sr);

How does the data look now with both the cloud cover filter and the cloud mask applied?









The image collection is now much cleaner and ready for analysis.
The dates and region selected here are intentional. The image precedes the destructive wildfires near Los Angeles in January 2025, which caused widespread damage across several communities. In the next exercise, we will use spectral band indices and change detection to map the extent and severity of this wildfire event and its impact on communities in the wildland-urban interface.

section: 10.7 Other Interfaces to the Earth Engine API
text:
10.7 Other Interfaces to the Earth Engine API
The Code Editor is the most convenient way to begin working with Earth Engine, but it is not the only one. The same Earth Engine backend can be accessed through several client libraries, each suited to a different workflow:








Interface
Language
Best for




Code Editor
JavaScript
Exploratory work, sharing scripts, learning GEE


earthengine-api
Python
Reproducible analysis, integration with Python scientific stack, batch processing


rgee
R
R-based workflows, integration with the R spatial ecosystem (sf, terra, stars)


REST API
Any
Production pipelines, web applications, languages without a client library



All four interfaces communicate with the same Earth Engine servers and produce identical results. The choice of interface is largely a matter of which ecosystem the rest of an analysis lives in.

10.7.1 The Python API
For analyses that combine Earth Engine outputs with other Python libraries (e.g., pandas, xarray, scikit-learn, geopandas), the Python API is the most natural fit. It is also the recommended interface for batch processing and scheduled jobs.

10.7.1.1 Installation
The python client library is named earthengine-api and can be installed through pip or conda:

# pip
pip install earthengine-api

# conda
conda install -c conda-forge earthengine-api

For interactive map display in Jupyter notebooks, the geemap package is strongly recommended. It provides a Code-Editor-like map widget and a number of convenient functions:

pip install geemap

If you are using Google Colab, both packages are pre-installed.


10.7.1.2 Authentication and Initialization
The Python API requires a one-time authentication step per machine, followed by initialization with a Cloud project ID at the start of each session:

import ee

# One-time per machine (opens a browser tab for OAuth)
ee.Authenticate()

# Required at the start of every session
ee.Initialize(project='your-project-id')

# Verify the connection
print(ee.String('Hello World!').getInfo())

The project argument should match the Cloud project ID created during account registration. If ee.Initialize() is called without a project argument, the call will fail with an error directing you to specify one.


10.7.1.3 A Parallel Example: Loading and Filtering an Image Collection
The Python API mirrors the JavaScript API closely. Object types, method names, and chaining patterns are nearly identical. The main syntactic differences are Python’s snake_case for some helper functions, the use of dictionaries instead of object literals, and the explicit getInfo() call required to pull values to the client.
The same Landsat 8 cloud-masked composite produced earlier in this chapter can be produced as follows:

import ee
import geemap

ee.Initialize(project='your-project-id')

# Cloud mask function - note the closer resemblance to the JS version
def mask_l8sr(image):
  qa = image.select('QA_PIXEL')
  cloud_mask = (qa.bitwiseAnd(1 << 1).eq(0) # Dilated cloud   
    .and(qa.bitwiseAnd(1 << 2).eq(0)) # Cirrus
    .and(qa.bitwiseAnd(1 << 3).eq(0)) # Cloud          
    .and(qa.bitwiseAnd(1 << 4).eq(0))) # Cloud shadow 
  return image.updateMask(cloud_mask)

# Define area of interest
geometry = ee.Geometry.Point([-118.64, 34.10])

# build the pre-fire composite
landsat_pre = (ee.ImageCollection('LANDSAT/LC08/C02/T1_L2')
               .filterBounds(geometry)
               .filterDate('2024-10-01', '2024-12-31')
               .filter(ee.Filter.lt('CLOUD_COVER', 20))
               .map(mask_l8sr)
               .median())
               
               
# Visualization parameters
true_color_vis = {
  'bands': ['SR_B4', 'SR_B3', 'SR_B2'],
  'min': 6000,
  'max': 19000
}

# Display in an interactive map
Map = geemap.Map()
Map.centerObject(geometry, 9)
Map.addLayer(landsat_pre, true_color_vis, 'Pre-Fire Image')
display(Map)

The structural similarity to the JavaScript version is intentional and reflects the fact that both client libraries are thin wrappers around the same underlying API.


10.7.1.4 Client vs. Server in Python
The client/server distinction introduced earlier in this chapter is particularly important to keep in mind when working in Python. Earth Engine objects are server-side: their values do not exist on the local machine and cannot be inspected directly with standard Python tools. For example, the following will not return what a Python user might expect:

# This prints a description of the server-side object, NOT its value
print(landsat_pre)

# this actually retrieves the value from the server
print(landsat_pre.bandNames().getInfo())

Calls to .getInfo() block execution until a response is received from the server, and can be slow or fail entirely for large objects. As a rule of thumb, getInfo() should be used sparingly and only on small, scalar results. For larger outputs, use ee.batch.Export to write results to Google Drive, Google Cloud Storage, or as Earth Engine Assets.



10.7.2 The R Interface: rgee
For users who prefer to remain in R, the rgee package provides an R binding for the Earth Engine API. rgee is a community-maintained package (part of the r-spatial ecosystem) rather than an official Google product, but it is well documented and stable, and integrates cleanly with the R spatial stack.
A practical caveat: rgee is implemented as a reticulate wrapper around the Python earthengine-api. This means that a working Python installation and the earthengine-api Python package are both required, even when working entirely in R. Setup is non-trivial on a fresh machine and is the most common source of friction reported by rgee users.
Installation and one-time setup:

install.packages("rgee")
library(rgee)

# installs Python dependencies (numpy, earthengine-api) into a managed Python environment
ee_install()

# one-time authentication
ee_Authentication()

Once installed, the syntax mirrors the Python API, with ee$ replacing ee for method access:

library(rgee)
ee_Initialize(project = "your-project-id")

first_image <- ee$Image("LANDSAT/LC08/C02/T1_L2/LC08_037035_20250619")

true_color_vis <- list(
  bands = c("SR_B4", "SR_B3", "SR_B2"),
  min = 8000,
  max = 18000
)

Map$addLayer(first_image, true_color_vis, "First Image")

For more on rgee, including examples of pulling Earth Engine outputs directly into sf and stars objects, see the package documentation at https://r-spatial.github.io/rgee/.


10.7.3 REST API
The REST API is the lowest-level interface to Earth Engine, exposing the service as a set of standard HTTPS endpoints that return JSON. Unlike the client libraries, the REST API has no language-specific bindings - it can be called from any environment capable of making authenticated HTTP requests, including web applications, mobile clients, or languages without a maintained Earth Engine library (e.g., Julia, Go, Rust).
For most analytical work, the REST API is not the recommended entry point. The JavaScript, Python, and R client libraries handle a substantial amount of complexity (object serialization, request batching, error handling) that must be implemented manually when working directly with REST. The REST API is most appropriate when:

Building a web application that needs to embed Earth Engine outputs
Integrating Earth Engine into a production pipeline written in a language without a client library
Calling Earth Engine from a serverless or edge environment where installing a full Python or Node.js stack is undesirable.

A minimal authenticated request to retrieve metadata for a single image might look like this in Python:

import requests
import google.auth
import google.auth.transport.requests

# get application default credentials (set up via `gcloud auth login`)
credentials, project = google.auth.default()
credentials.refresh(google.auth.transport.requests.Request())

# construct the request
asset_id = 'LANDSAT/LC08/C02/T1_L2/LC08_037035_20250619'
url = f'https://earthengine.googleapis.com/v1/projects/{project}/assets/{asset_id}'

response = requests.get(
  url,
  headers = {'Authorization': f'Bearer {credentials.token}'}
)

print(response.json())

REST authentication is handled through standard Google Cloud OAuth2 flows and supports both user accounts and service accounts. Service accounts are typically preferred for automated or unattended workflows.
Full documentation of available endpoints is provided in the GEE REST API Reference.

title: 11  One Health, Pathogen Surveillance, and Nextstrain
section: 11.1 Introduction: What is One Health, and why is it important?
text:
11.1 Introduction: What is One Health, and why is it important?
Infectious disease dynamics emerge from the complex interactions among host species, pathogens, and the environments they inhabit. Increasingly, ecologists and public health researchers recognize that these interactions cannot be understood by studying human, animal, or environmental health in isolation.
The One Health framework gained major momentum in 2004 when the Wildlife Conservation Society generated the “Manhattan Principles” to guide zoonotic infectious disease management (https://www.oneworldonehealth.org/sept2004/owoh_sept04.html). The principles hoped to address the complex interactions between hosts, pathogen, and their environments, while focusing on minimizing the threat to the health of life on Earth. This followed major international zoonotic outbreaks, including: West Nile Virus, Ebola, SARS, Monkeypox, Mad Cow Disease, and Avian Influenza. The principles emphasized the intricate dynamics influencing infectious disease transmission and behavior, and recognized that the health of humans, non-human animals, and ecosystems is fundamentally interconnected. At its core, One Health is both a conceptual framework and a collaborative and interdisciplinary approach that integrates experts from a diverse range of fields such as ecology, veterinary medicine, epidemiology, wildlife disease ecology, public health, and environmental science with the goal of working together to better understand and manage disease risk.



This info-graphic was created by One-Health High Level Expert Panel (OHHLEP) to support the definition for One Health. OHHLEP is an integrated advisory panel with members from the The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), the World Organisation for Animal Health (OIE), the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) and the World Health Organization (WHO). Image source: https://www.who.int/news/item/01-12-2021-tripartite-and-unep-support-ohhlep-s-definition-of-one-health


One Health has become especially important in an era of rapid environmental change. Climate warming, land-use change, biodiversity loss, urbanization, and global movement of people and goods can all alter opportunities for pathogen transmission and emergence. Many of these drivers influence the ecology of zoonotic diseases, i.e., infectious diseases that are transmitted among wildlife or domestic animals/livestock, and with the potential to spillover into human hosts.
A substantial proportion of emerging infectious diseases in humans originate from animal hosts (an organism or species that can harbor a pathogen and act as a long-term, natural source of infection), which highlights the importance of integrated approaches to surveillance and prevention. The COVID-19 pandemic further underscored the global consequences of emerging pathogens while revealing both the value and limitations of disease surveillance systems operating across political and ecological boundaries. The pandemic accelerated interest in One Health and the coordinated, data-driven approaches to disease surveillance and management, and helped bring renewed attention to One Health as both an important research paradigm and policy framework.
Global efforts from international organizations have increasingly emphasized One Health, for more information, see:

Global One Health Community (GOHC) https://globalohc.org/
World Health Organization (WHO) https://www.who.int/health-topics/one-health#tab=tab_1
Center for Disease Control (CDC) https://www.cdc.gov/one-health/about/index.html
One Health Initiative (OHI) https://onehealthinitiative.com/

In addition, One Health is increasingly referenced and cited in the scientific community, for more information, see: (Mackenzie and Jeggo 2019; (OHHLEP) et al. 2022; Zinsstag et al. 2011; Destoumieux-Garzón et al. 2018; Queenan et al. 2017), and the official One Health scientific journal, from the International Federation of Tropical Medicine https://www.sciencedirect.com/journal/one-health
For more information on One Health, the following video produced by the World Organisation for Animal Health gives a brief overview of the concept, and especially focuses on how changing environmental conditions can lead to altered zoonotic pathogen dynamics:


Another great resource for more information on One Health comes from a Ted Talk by Dr. Sharon Deem, a DVM and PhD with a unique perspective on the effects of environmental disruptions that could lead to spillover of zoonotic pathogens into humans. Notably, this talk was given in June 2018, just months before the start of the COVID-19 pandemic.


Although often discussed conceptually, One Health increasingly depends on data availability, and requires knowledge of tools in informatics and big-data management. Monitoring disease risks across host species, vector populations (i.e, intermediary hosts that can transmit pathogens, like mosquitoes or ticks), landscapes, ecosystems, and climates, requires integrating diverse information streams, often in near real time. This challenge makes One Health not only a biological framework, but also an informatics problem.

title: 11  One Health, Pathogen Surveillance, and Nextstrain
section: 11.2 One Health as an Ecoinformatics Problem
text:
11.2 One Health as an Ecoinformatics Problem
Because disease systems operate across ecological, spatial, and temporal scales, studying them often requires integrating many types of data. This is where ecoinformatics plays an increasingly important role in One Health approaches.
Ecoinformatics applies computational, statistical, and data-science approaches to ecological questions, often leveraging large, heterogeneous, and spatially explicit datasets. For disease ecology and zoonotic management, these tools can help integrate information across multiple dimensions of a pathogen transmission system, including:

Host data, such as wildlife spatial distributions, abundance, movement dynamics, etc.
Vector surveillance data, including movement, fecundity or health of vector populations possible infection prevalence.
Environmental/Climate data, such as temperature, precipitation, vegetation, land-use, etc., and how these vary spatially and temporally (annual patterns and/or seasonal patterns)
Geospatial data products, leveraged data products that can be used to identify potential hotspots (where disease transmission is more/most likely), model risk to human hosts, and possibly forecast future outbreaks.

Viewed through this lens, many One Health questions become problems of data integration. For example; How do climatic anomalies or phenological patterns influence vector-borne disease outbreaks? How does landscape fragmentation alter opportunities for spillover into human hosts? Can environmental and surveillance data be combined to forecast and predict emerging disease risk, pinpointing potential areas with higher likelihood of disease outbreaks? Addressing these questions often requires combining ecological data collected at different spatial and temporal scales, a central challenge in many ecoinformatics research questions.
Geospatial analysis and results are particularly important because many disease processes are inherently spatial. Vector distributions shift across landscapes, reservoir hosts migrate, and environmental suitability for transmission can vary among regions or ecosystems, and can change over time. Mapping and modeling the dynamics of pathogen that cause disease in humans can reveal patterns difficult or impossible to detect through case counts and clinical data alone.
In this way, ecoinformatics and big-data research pipelines can provide much of the analytical foundation needed to practically apply One Health approaches. A major challenge is not only collecting these data streams, but making them interoperable and reproducible across disciplines. Rather than treating disease ecology as separate from environmental and earth data science, One Health can be viewed as an important tool toward pathogen surveillance and management, with informatics as the common thread connecting the diverse disciplines needed.

title: 11  One Health, Pathogen Surveillance, and Nextstrain
text:
11.3 Case Study: West Nile Virus

11.3.0.1 Background Information for WNV
To illustrate these ideas, and analyze a specific example of One Health in practice, we focus this chapter on West Nile Virus (WNV), which is a vector-borne zoonotic pathogen that highlights many of the ecological and surveillance challenges that have motivated One Health approaches.
WNV is an important viral pathogen that can cause severe disease in humans and several other animal hosts. The pathogen was first introduced into the United States in the late 1990’s, and has since spread throughout North America. In humans, the individuals that become symptomatic (around 20% of those infected) develop flu-like symptoms, including fever, headache, body aches, fatigue, and sometimes a rash. In addition, a small proportion of cases (less than 1%) can cause extremely severe neuroinvasive disease that can cause stupor, disorientation, coma, tremors, convulsion, and even paralysis. (Petersen et al. 2013)
West Nile Virus is maintained through transmission cycles primarily involving different species of birds as the major reservoir host, and mosquitoes, particularly species in the Culex genus, as vectors. Humans and other mammals may become infected through mosquito bites but are generally considered incidental/accidental, or “dead-end” hosts, because they typically do not contribute to onward transmission.



Graphic depicting the transmission cycle of West Nile Virus. Mosquitoes and several different bird species circulate the pathogen, where mosquitoes will become vectors of the pathogen by biting infected birds, and bird hosts become infected by being bit by infected mosquito vectors. Incidental/accidental hosts can then become infected if they are bit by an infected mosquito vector, leading to spillover to humans. Image source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK544246/figure/article-31340.image.f1/


This multihost transmission cycle makes WNV a classic One Health system: transmission dynamics emerge through interactions among wildlife hosts, vector ecology, environmental conditions, and human exposure. Importantly, WNV (and other vector-borne diseases) have become increasingly studied in the interface between climate change and zoonotic pathogen research due to changing global environmental conditions that can often favor mosquito habitat (Mordecai et al. 2019).


11.3.0.2 Why West Nile Virus in the Desert Southwest?
The desert Southwest, specifically the state of Arizona, provides a particularly relevant setting for exploring these dynamics.
Environmental conditions in arid and semi-arid systems can strongly shape mosquito abundance, host movement, and pathogen amplification. Temperature influences mosquito development rates, viral replication within vectors, and transmission potential, while precipitation and hydrological variability can affect fecundity and breeding habitat availability.
These links make WNV especially relevant in the context of climate variability and climate change. Warming temperatures, altered drought regimes, and changing precipitation patterns may influence both the timing and geography of disease risk.
Arizona also provides a useful regional case study because mosquito-borne disease dynamics occur in a range of diverse ecological contexts, from urban desert environments to the riparian corridors used by many host species. This ecological heterogeneity creates opportunities to explore how spatial variation can influence disease surveillance and management.
For more information on West Nile Virus in Arizona, see: (Landau and Leeuwen 2012; Jobe et al. 2024; Wilke et al. 2023; Coalson et al. 2023)
Because transmission dynamics are shaped by environmental conditions, host communities and populations, and vector ecology, West Nile Virus offers a powerful example of how One Health concepts can intersect with geospatial data and ecoinformatics tools, and provide critical insight to possibly predicting public health risks from disease.

title: 11  One Health, Pathogen Surveillance, and Nextstrain
section: 11.4 Nextstrain: A Research Infrastructure for Pathogen Surveillance
text:
11.4 Nextstrain: A Research Infrastructure for Pathogen Surveillance
Understanding and managing disease risk increasingly depends on open and interoperable research infrastructure. One important example is Nextstrain https://nextstrain.org/ (Hadfield et al. (2018)), which is an open-source platform for real-time tracking of pathogen evolution and spatial spread for numerous pathogens, including Avian Influenza, Rabies, SARS-CoV-2, and West Nile Virus.
Nextstrain combines pathogen genomic data with phylogenetic analysis, temporal information, and geographic metadata to visualize how pathogens move and diversify/mutate through populations over time. Originally developed for outbreak tracking and genomic epidemiology and phylogenetic inference, the platform has become an important example of modern pathogen surveillance infrastructure with publicly available open-source data.
Rather than treating pathogen genomes as isolated sequences, Nextstrain combines the available sequences and places them together in a spatial and evolutionary context, enabling researchers to ask questions such as:

How are pathogen lineages spreading geographically?
Are outbreaks linked through shared genetic ancestry?
How does pathogen genetic diversity change over time?
Can genomic surveillance complement traditional epidemiological monitoring?

These questions align closely with One Health objectives in integrating biological, environmental, and spatial information. During the COVID-19 pandemic, genomic surveillance platforms and pathogen research infrastructure played important roles in tracking viral evolution in near real time, by collecting and combining international sequence data. Throughout the course of the pandemic, different isolated genetic strains/variants of the SARS-CoV-2 virus spread rapidly (e.g., Omicron, Delta, Gamma, etc.), each with varying characteristics and behavior affecting pathogen transmission, disease severity, and vaccine evasion. Collaborative efforts were maximized by the use and application of open-source platforms like Nextstrain, allowing the sharing and reproducibility of a wide range of data. The same principles applied during the COVID-19 pandemic can and do extend beyond pandemic pathogens to the management and surveillance of zoonotic and vector-borne diseases, like West Nile Virus.
Importantly, genomic surveillance of zoonotic pathogens does not replace traditional environmental surveillance or earth sciences. Rather, it complements other research infrastructures, including:

Wildlife/insect surveillance networks (e.g., population surveys, insect prevalence, etc.)
Public health case reporting systems (e.g., CDC clinical case reports, county health data, etc.)
Environmental and climate monitoring products (e.g., NEON, USGS, etc.)
Geospatial mapping tools (e.g., NASA EOS, NEON AOP, etc.)

Together, these resources form part of a more broad One Health surveillance ecosystem. In this chapter, we use Nextstrain as an example of how open-source research infrastructure supports modern disease ecology and pathogen management efforts. Although genomic surveillance offers one lens on pathogen dynamics, many surveillance questions begin with simpler spatial data products and analysis. We next explore how geospatial mapping of case data can provide a complementary and fundamental One Health tool.
The coding exercise that follows focuses on a critical component of surveillance efforts, mapping the spatial distribution of a pathogen (here, West Nile Virus in Arizona) using publicly available data in R.

title: 11  One Health, Pathogen Surveillance, and Nextstrain
section: 11.5 Coding Lab 1: Utilizing WNV Data from Nextstrain for Mapping Sampling Intensity in Arizona
text:
11.5 Coding Lab 1: Utilizing WNV Data from Nextstrain for Mapping Sampling Intensity in Arizona

11.5.1 Overview
In this exercise, we will use openly available pathogen surveillance data from Nextstrain to:

Access publically available data in Nextstrain through R
Import and inspect genomic surveillance metadata in R
Real world data-cleaning and management of messy data
Create a simple spatial visualization of West Nile Virus observations
Aggregate the observations into a county-level map in Arizona

This exercise introduces a simple but reproducible workflow for working with pathogen surveillance infrastructure in R to address a part of a One Health approach in the management of West Nile Virus.


11.5.2 Part 1: Install and Load Required Packages
Before beginning our analysis, we need to install and load the R packages required for this exercise. The following code checks whether each package is already installed and installs only those that are missing.

#######################################
# Install packages (only if needed)
#######################################

packages <- c(
  "tidyverse",  # data wrangling and visualization
  "sf",         # spatial data
  "tigris",     # US Census boundary data
  "stringr",    # text manipulation
  "maps",       # mapping
  "zstd"        # decompress Zstandard (.zst) files
)

# Identify packages that are not already installed
missing_packages <- packages[
  !packages %in% rownames(installed.packages())
]

# Install only missing packages
if (length(missing_packages) > 0) {
  install.packages(missing_packages)
}

Load packages into our R session:

#######################################
# Load packages
#######################################

library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(tigris)
library(stringr)
library(maps)
library(zstd)



11.5.3 Part 2: Access Nextstrain Data

11.5.3.1 About Nextstrain data access
Analysis and visualization of publicly available data on Nextstrain is possible on their website (<nextstrain.org>), but it is also possible to complete your own analyses or visualization with the help of their open-source software and robust documentation using R, Python, and other computational tools.
Here https://docs.nextstrain.org/en/latest/index.html is where you can find tutorials on installing tools, analyzing pathogen genomes, creating your own phylogenetic trees and workflows, or even how to upload your own pathogen genome sequences to be integrated to their website. The documentation includes instructions whether your system operator is macOS, Windows, or Linux.
Many Nextstrain datasets are distributed as machine-readable JSON files (similar to other research infrastructure datasets we have accessed through this course). For example, genomic sequence data are commonly provided in FASTA format (.fasta), while the associated metadata may be provided in tab-separated values (.tsv) or compressed formats such as Zstandard (.zst). See the Nextstrain documentation for additional examples, file formats and their applications, and more information.
To explore the available datasets, use this link: https://nextstrain.org/pathogens/files to search through all available pathogens and downloadable data files on Nextstrain.
For this exercise, we will work with metadata associated with West Nile virus (WNV). The metadata file contains information associated with the WNV sequences available through Nextstrain, including geographic information about the source of each sequence. We will download this file directly from Nextstrain’s public data endpoint and use it to explore the geographic distribution of available WNV sequence data.


11.5.3.2 Downloading and decompressing the metadata file
The WNV metadata file is distributed as a Zstandard-compressed file (.zst). Compression reduces file size, making datasets easier and faster to distribute. Before we can import the metadata into R, we first need to decompress the downloaded file.
We can accomplish both steps directly in R using the download.file() function and the zstd package. The following code downloads the compressed metadata file, decompresses it, and saves the resulting tab-separated values file (.tsv) to our working directory.

##################################################
# Download and decompress West Nile virus metadata
##################################################

# Define file names
metadata_url <- "https://data.nextstrain.org/files/workflows/WNV/metadata.tsv.zst"
compressed_file <- "wnv_metadata.tsv.zst"
metadata_file <- "wnv_metadata.tsv"

# Download the compressed metadata file
download.file(
  url = metadata_url,
  destfile = compressed_file,
  mode = "wb"
)

# Check that the download succeeded
if (!file.exists(compressed_file) || file.size(compressed_file) == 0) {
  stop("Metadata download failed. Please check your internet connection and try again.")
}

# Decompress the .zst file
zstd::zstd_decompress(
  compressed_file,
  metadata_file
)

# Check that decompression succeeded
if (!file.exists(metadata_file)) {
  stop("Metadata decompression failed. Please check the downloaded file.")
}

After running this code, we should have two files in our working directory: the original compressed file (wnv_metadata.tsv.zst) and the decompressed metadata file (wnv_metadata.tsv). The decompressed .tsv file is the version we will use for the remainder of this exercise.


11.5.3.3 Loading and exploring the metadata
Now that the metadata file has been downloaded and decompressed, we can import it into our R environment using read.delim(). Because the file is tab-separated, we specify “ as the delimiter.

###############################################
# Read West Nile virus metadata
###############################################

wnv_metadata <- read.delim(
  metadata_file,
  sep = "\t",
  header = TRUE
)

The metadata is now stored in our R environment as an object called wnv_metadata. We can begin by inspecting the first few rows using the head() function. This is a useful initial check to confirm that the data have been imported correctly.

######################################################
# Sanity check: Do the data look as expected?
######################################################

head(wnv_metadata)

  accession       date region country division location state          host
1  PZ019009 2024-07-15 Europe Germany   Berlin                Culex pipiens
2  PZ019010 2024-07-16 Europe Germany   Berlin                Culex pipiens
3  PZ019011 2024-07-15 Europe Germany   Berlin                Culex pipiens
4  PZ019012 2024-07-17 Europe Germany   Berlin                Culex pipiens
5  PZ019013 2024-07-18 Europe Germany   Berlin                Culex pipiens
6  PZ019014 2024-07-18 Europe Germany   Berlin                Culex pipiens
  host_genus host_type is_lab_host                authors
1      Culex  Mosquito             Patzina-Mehling et al.
2      Culex  Mosquito             Patzina-Mehling et al.
3      Culex  Mosquito             Patzina-Mehling et al.
4      Culex  Mosquito             Patzina-Mehling et al.
5      Culex  Mosquito             Patzina-Mehling et al.
6      Culex  Mosquito             Patzina-Mehling et al.
                                            url length clade_membership lineage
1 https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/nuccore/PZ019009  10573                        2
2 https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/nuccore/PZ019010  10573                        2
3 https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/nuccore/PZ019011  10573                        2
4 https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/nuccore/PZ019012  10573                        2
5 https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/nuccore/PZ019013  10570                        2
6 https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/nuccore/PZ019014  10573                        2


The output shows the first six observations in our dataset. We can also examine the dimensions of the dataset to determine how many observations and variables it contains:

###############################################
# Examine the dimensions of the dataset
###############################################

dim(wnv_metadata)

[1] 25421    16


In this case, the metadata contains 25,417 observations with 16 variables. Each observation represents a sequence record, while the variables contain additional information associated with that record.
To better understand what information is available, we can examine the variable names using the names() function:

###############################################
# What information does the metadata file have? 
###############################################

names(wnv_metadata)

 [1] "accession"        "date"             "region"           "country"         
 [5] "division"         "location"         "state"            "host"            
 [9] "host_genus"       "host_type"        "is_lab_host"      "authors"         
[13] "url"              "length"           "clade_membership" "lineage"         


Here, we see a variety of information related to all observations in our dataset, including:

a unique identifier for each sample (“accession”)
date of collection(“date”)
several columns related to geographic data (“region”, “country”, “division”, “location”, “state”)
data related to the host species where the virus was detected (“host”, “host_genus”, “host_type”, “is_lab_host”)
sample source (i.e., who and where the data was published, “authors”, “url”)
phenotype information (“length”, “lineage”, “clade_membership”)

All of these data can be relevant for a variety of research questions, especially in the context of One Health related objectives.



11.5.4 Part 3: Filtering to Arizona Observations
Here, we want to focus on geographic information, starting with filtering to just Arizona data:

##################################################
# Filter our metadata to just Arizona observations
##################################################

az_wnv_data <- wnv_metadata %>% 
  filter(state == "AZ")    

# Note: Inspecting the original metadata is crucial for making sure your 
# naming definition is correct. Here, state-level labeling is also consistent
# with the division-level filtering, both resulting in the same output.

Take a look at the data, unfortunately, only a subset of the Arizona data has more precise location data. Let’s filter out columns that do not have any location data.

##########################################
# Filter out blanks from 'location' column
##########################################

az_wnv_filtered <- az_wnv_data %>% 
  filter(location != "")

Now that we have our data subset to include just Arizona data with reliable precise location data, let’s inspect the remaining location column to determine our next steps:

######################################################
# unique() shows all unique names in 'location' column
######################################################

unique(az_wnv_filtered$location)

[1] "Gilbert"       "Glendale"      "Phoenix"       "Tempe Az"     
[5] "Cochise Co."   "Maricopoa Co." "Apache Co."   


Perfect, this is messy (but fixable) real-world surveillance data. Our filtering process to precise locations for Arizona samples ends up with some data reported at the city level with different naming schemes, and some at the county level. Importantly, we also see that there is a typo in the data (“Maricopoa Co.” instead of “Maricopa Co.”). The next step is a crucial component to all ecoinformatics pipelines, data cleaning.
Let’s use dplyr and stringr to convert all location data to workable formats. NOTE: depending on your data, this process may change:

########################
#Clean text and fix typo
########################

az_wnv_filtered <- az_wnv_filtered %>% 
  mutate(
    location_clean = str_trim(location),
    location_clean = str_to_title(location_clean),
    location_clean = str_replace(location_clean, " Co\\.", ""),
    location_clean = str_replace_all(location_clean, "Maricopoa", "Maricopa")
  )

########################
# Fix messy strings
########################

az_wnv_filtered <- az_wnv_filtered %>% 
  mutate(
    location_clean = case_when(
      location_clean == "Tempe Az" ~ "Tempe",
      TRUE ~ location_clean
    )
  )

##############################
# Translate cities to counties
##############################

az_wnv_filtered <- az_wnv_filtered %>% 
  mutate(
    county = case_when(
      location_clean %in% c("Phoenix", "Glendale", "Gilbert", "Tempe") ~ "Maricopa",
      location_clean == "Maricopa" ~ "Maricopa",
      location_clean == "Cochise" ~ "Cochise",
      location_clean == "Apache" ~ "Apache",
      TRUE ~ location_clean
    )
  )

###########################
# Sanity check our workflow
###########################

table(az_wnv_filtered$location_clean)


  Apache  Cochise  Gilbert Glendale Maricopa  Phoenix    Tempe 
       1        1       11        2        1        2       10 


Now, we have 7 discrete and unique locations (some county-level, some city-level). Let’s formally aggregate the data and assign approximate coordinates to each point to continue with our analysis and generate a map:

##########################################################
# wnv_az_points to aggregate number of points per location
##########################################################

wnv_az_points <- az_wnv_filtered %>% 
  group_by(location_clean) %>% 
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

#############################################
# Assign lat/long centroids per each location
#############################################

coords <- data.frame(
  location_clean = c("Gilbert", "Glendale", "Phoenix", "Tempe", "Cochise", "Apache", "Maricopa"),
  lat = c(33.3528, 33.5387, 33.4484, 33.4255, 31.8795, 35.3851, 33.2918),
  lon = c(-111.7890, -112.1860, -112.0740, -111.9400, -109.7515, -109.5390, -112.4291)
)

###################################
# Join wnv_az_points to coordinates
###################################

wnv_az_geospatial <- left_join(wnv_az_points, coords, by = "location_clean")

Now, we have a dataframe (wnv_az_geospatial) that includes the sample location (city or county), the number of samples collected at that location, and the approximate coordinates of where that observations was collected/reported. Because surveillance data are often unevenly samples across space, we aggregate sequence metadata into approximate geographic centroids to visualize sampling intensity across administrative regions (cities and/or counties).
Importantly, our results will reflect the sampling intensity rather than true disease prevalence. In other words, locations with more recorded samples may reflect differences in surveillance efforts, sequencing/sampling effort or capacity, or resources and reporting infrastructure rather than higher actual rates of West Nile Virus transmission. Epidemiologists and disease ecologists must grapple with and carefully account for how social, logistical, and institutional factors could influence and shape the structure of available data, extrapolating those results in meaningful ways, and interpret spatial patterns of disease. From a One Health perspective, this highlights how the interdisciplinary forces (biological, environmental, socio-institutional/cultural, etc.) jointly shape the data used to infer infectious disease dynamics, and why careful interpretation is necessary when translating surveillance data into conclusions about disease risk. Our work here is one piece of the broader framework used in pathogen surveillance and management.


11.5.5 Part 4: Visualization of our results
Let’s generate a map to visualize our work:

############################
# Use ggplot to create a map
############################

arizona_wnv_map <- ggplot(wnv_az_geospatial) + 
  
  # --- Base map: Arizona + counties ---
  annotation_borders("state", regions = "arizona",
                     fill = "gray96", color = "gray60") +
  
  annotation_borders("county", regions = "arizona",
                     color = "white", alpha = 0.5) +
  
  # --- Data layer ---
  geom_point(
    aes(x = lon, y = lat, size = n, color = n),
    shape = 19,
    alpha = 1
  ) +
  
  # --- Coordinate system ---
  coord_fixed(1.3) +
  
  # --- Size scaling ---
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(2.5, 9)) +
  
  # --- Viridis color scale ---
  scale_color_viridis_c(
    option = "viridis",
    name = "Sample count"
  ) +
  
  # --- Labels ---
  labs(
    title = "West Nile Virus Surveillance Intensity in Arizona",
    subtitle = "Point size and color reflect number of samples per location",
    size = "Sample count"
  ) +
  
  # --- Theme ---
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(
      hjust = 0.5,
      face = "bold",
      size = 18
    ),
    
    plot.subtitle = element_text(
      hjust = 0.5,
      size = 12,
      color = "gray30"
    ),
    
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    
    axis.title = element_blank(),
    axis.text = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    
    legend.position = "right",
    
    legend.title = element_text(size = 11),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 10)
  ) +
  
  guides(size = "none")

arizona_wnv_map

section: 11.6 Coding Lab 2: Temporal Application of the WNV Dataset in the United States
text:
11.6 Coding Lab 2: Temporal Application of the WNV Dataset in the United States
The coding lab above shows an important application of determining potential localized areas where further research is necessary (especially the conditions that influence high sampling intensity near Maricopa County). Another important epidemiological application for this dataset would be to investigate the temporal relationship of West Nile Virus spread throughout the country following the initial introduction to the western hemisphere. The first detection of WNV in the United States occurred in New York state in 1999, following its introduction from its endemic region in Africa and the Middle East, likely from an infected bird, human, or mosquito. (Petersen et al. (2013)). Here, in Coding Lab 2, we expand our spatial scale to examine the early spread of WNV across the United States.
Using the original complete Nextstrain metadata, we can estimate the earliest recorded detection year for each state to visualize the temporal progression and relationship of the outbreak, and map the spread of the pathogen over time following the initial introduction. This is an important analysis for many epidemiologists and One Health scientists. Rather than mapping all individual observations (which can be sparse and uneven through time), we estimate the earliest recorded detection year for each US state using the Nextstrain metadata.

11.6.1 Part 1: Filter our original metadata
First, we revert back to our originally downloaded metadata file, saved as wnv_metadata, and filter this dataset to only include observations from the United States

###############################################
# Filter metadata to United States observations
###############################################

us_wnv <- wnv_metadata %>% 
  filter(country == "USA")

And now, we can extract the year from the collection data variable. Within the metadata file, there includes a full data field, typically in the YYYY-MM-DD format. To focus on the temporal spread, we extract just the year from each observation.

#######################################
# Extract the year from the data column
#######################################

us_wnv <- us_wnv %>% 
  mutate(
    year = as.numeric(substr(date, 1, 4))
  )

We have now created a new dataset (us_wnv) that only includes US observations (reducing the total number from 25,202 in the original metadata file, down to 5,149 observations), with a newly created variable, ‘year’ that reports just the year from each observation.


11.6.2 Part 2: Exploring temporal patterns in the dataset
Before aggregating the data to first detection year by state, it is useful to explore how sampling effort varies through time. Understanding temporal patterns in the dataset helps contextualize the spatial results, and highlights an important challenge in disease ecology: distinguishing true ecological patterns from variation in sampling intensity.
In addition, the metadata include information on the host type (e.g., birds, mosquitoes), allowing us to examine how different components of the complex transmission cycle of WNV are represented in the dataset over time.
To visualize these patterns, we can create a simple plot that shows how the number of samples in the dataset changes through time, while also distinguishing among host types (host_type is a variable included in the metadata). This allows us to explore both temporal variation in sampling effort and how different components of the WNV transmission cycle are represented in the data.

######################################################
# Filter out missing samples for year and/or host type
######################################################

us_wnv_plot <- us_wnv %>% 
  filter(!is.na(year), !is.na(host_type), host_type != "")

#######################################################################
# Quick look at the host_type data to see if we need to do any cleaning
#######################################################################

unique(us_wnv_plot$host_type)

[1] "Mosquito"       "Human"          "Other"          "Bird"          
[5] "Nans"           "Psorophora sp." "Astur gentilis" "Horse"         


Looking at each of the unique values reported in the host_type column, we see several unique values, but also some data cleanup we need to do first. Importantly, “Psorophora sp.” represents a genus of Mosquitoes, and “Astur gentilis” represents the goshawk, a raptor/bird species. These should be combined. Also, “Nans” seems to be an reporting error consistent in a large set of data submitted to Nextstrain. A quick look through the metadata file, and following the publication url shows that all data with the “Nans” host type are also all collected from birds, and should also be combined.

########################################
# Clean and combine host_type categories
########################################

us_wnv_plot <- us_wnv_plot %>% 
  mutate(
    host_type_clean = case_when(
      # Birds
      host_type %in% c("Bird", "Astur gentilis", "Nans") ~ "Bird",
      # Mosquitoes
      host_type %in% c("Mosquito", "Psorophora sp.") ~ "Mosquito",
      # Humans
      host_type == "Human" ~ "Human",
      # Horse
      host_type == "Horse" ~ "Horse",
      # Everything else
      TRUE ~ "Other"
    )
  ) %>% 
  filter(!is.na(host_type_clean))

Now, we can create a simple stacked bar plot, including number of sampled reported in the US each year, divided into the proportion of each year’s samples that represent the different host types recorded.

##################
# Stacked bar plot
##################

wnv_time_host_plot <- ggplot(us_wnv_plot,
                             aes(x = year, fill = host_type_clean)) + 
  
  geom_bar(position = "stack") + 
  
  labs(
    title = "West Nile Virus Sampling Through Time by Host Type",
    subtitle = "Nextstrain metadata from the United States",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Number of Samples",
    fill = "Host Type"
  ) + 
  
  theme_bw(base_size = 13) + 
  
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(
      hjust = 0.5,
      face = "bold",
      size = 16
    ),
    
    plot.subtitle = element_text(
      hjust = 0.5,
      size = 11,
      color = "gray30"
    ),
    
    legend.position = "right",
    legend.title = element_text(size = 11),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 10)
  )

wnv_time_host_plot








This figure highlights how sampling effort varies through time and across host types. In several years, the number of available samples increases substantially, reflecting changes in surveillance intensity, sequencing capacity, and research priorities rather than true changes in disease prevalence alone.
Additionally, the distribution of samples across host types illustrates the multi-host nature of West Nile Virus transmission. Observations include both avian reservoir hosts and mosquito vectors, reinforcing a key principle of One Health: understanding disease dynamics requires integrating information across multiple species and components of the transmission system.
Importantly, these temporal and host-related patterns influence how we interpret spatial analyses. Uneven sampling through time can affect estimates of when and where a pathogen is first detected, motivating the use of simplified epidemiological metrics such as what follows in the subsequent section.


11.6.3 Part 3: Determine first detection for each state
The next step is to determine which observation per each state was the first detection, so we can determine the first detection year for all states that have reported observations of WNV. This will reduce noise from uneven sampling (both temporally and spatially).

##################################################
# Calculate earliest detection year for each state
##################################################

first_detection <- us_wnv %>% 
  filter(!is.na(year)) %>% 
  group_by(state) %>% 
  summarise(
    first_year = min(year),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

Let’s look at our dataset, specifically, let’s look at what the “state” variable and the unique characters in our new dataset:

###################################################
# How many unique observations in 'state' variable?
###################################################

unique(first_detection$state)

 [1] "AR" "AZ" "CA" "CO" "CT" "FL" "GA" "IA" "ID" "IL" "IN" "LA" "MA" "MN" "MO"
[16] "MS" "ND" "NE" "NH" "NJ" "NM" "NV" "NY" "OH" "OK" "OR" "PA" "SC" "SD" "TN"
[31] "TX" "UT" "VA" "WA" "WI" "WY"




11.6.4 Part 4: Preparing state data for our visualization
Above, we see that there are 36 unique states available for our dataset. Importantly, these data report the state with the unique two-letter abbreviations(e.g., Arizona is “AZ”). The map_data available through ggplot2 and the tidyverse uses full lowercase names (e.g., Arizona is “arizona”). We need to match the state abbreviations to full lowercase names:

###############################
# First, load US state map data
###############################

states_map <- map_data("state")

###########################
# Create state lookup table
###########################

state_lookup <- data.frame(
  state = state.abb,
  state_name = tolower(state.name)
)

#####################################
# Join lookup table to detection data
#####################################

first_detection <- first_detection %>% 
  left_join(state_lookup, by = "state")

###############################################
# Now, join detection data to map_data polygons
###############################################

map_data_joined <- states_map %>% 
  left_join(first_detection, by = c("region" = "state_name"))



11.6.5 Part 5: Visualize the temporal progression of WNV across the United States
Now, we’re ready to plot our results in a national US map for all available states with data:

########################################
# Plot first detection year by state
########################################

us_wnv_map <- ggplot(map_data_joined, 
                     aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group, fill = first_year)) +
  
  geom_polygon(color = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  
  coord_fixed(1.3) +
  
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    option = "rocket",
    na.value = "gray90",
    name = "First detection year"
  ) +
  
  labs(
    title = "Spread of West Nile Virus Across the United States",
    subtitle = "Earliest recorded detection year by state (Nextstrain metadata)"
  ) +
  
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold", size = 18),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 12, color = "gray30"),
    
    axis.title = element_blank(),
    axis.text = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    
    legend.position = "right",
    legend.title = element_text(size = 11),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 10)
  )

us_wnv_map








The map illustrates the temporal spread of West Nile Virus across the United States, beginning with its introduction in 1999 and expanding across states in subsequent years. Taken as a whole, it seems that the earliest detection years were in the east coast, and spreading west over time. Washington state in the upper pacific northwest region has the latest detection year in the Nextstrain dataset. States filled in gray have no available data reported or published.
However, as with the Arizona case study from Coding Lab 1, it is important to interpret these patterns carefully:

The “first detection year” reflects the recorded observations, but that doesn’t necessarily reflect the true first arrival of the pathogen
Again, as with the Arizona case study, differences among states may reflect sampling effort, availability of surveillance infrastructure, or sequencing capacity, rather than biological spread alone. As such, some states may appear to have later detection simply due to delayed reporting or limited data availability.

Connection back to One Health, this national-scale perspective complements our earlier regional analysis by showing how:

Pathogen spread occurs across large spatial scales
Surveillance data are shaped by human systems and infrastructure
Integrating spatial and temporal data is essential for understanding zoonotic disease dynamics

Together, these case studies can highlight an important and central challenge in One Health initiatives; distinguishing true ecological patterns from the structure and limitations of the data used to observe/report them.

title: 11  One Health, Pathogen Surveillance, and Nextstrain
text:
11.7 One Health/Nextstrain Written Questions:
1. Sampling intensity vs. ecological signal (Arizona focus): The Arizona map shows a strong clustering of samples in Maricopa County. What mechanisms could produce this pattern? How might you distinguish between true ecological drivers (e.g., mosquito abundance, host density, climate/habitat suitability) and sampling biases (e.g., urban surveillance infrastructure, reporting effort, interest)?
2. Human systems as part of disease ecology (One Health lens): How do human factors, such as population density, public health funding, and access to sequencing technologies, shape the spatial and temporal patterns observed in pathogen datasets like this one? In what ways are these human systems an integral part of disease ecology itself?
3. Temporal sampling patterns and external events: The stacked bar plot shows variation in sampling through time, including a noticeable drop in recent years (2019 - now). What are some possible explanations for this pattern (e.g., changes in funding, shifting public health priorities during the COVID-19 pandemic, or true changes in WNV prevalence)? How would you test these competing hypotheses?
4. Host representation and transmission dynamics: The dataset includes samples from multiple host types (e.g., birds, mosquitoes, humans). How does the relative representation of these host types influence our understanding of the WNV transmission cycle? What biases might arise if one host group is oversampled relative to others?
5. Interpreting spread using first detection maps: The US map visualizes the first recorded detection year of WNV by state. What are the strengths and limitations of using first detection as a metric for pathogen spread? How might uneven surveillance effort across states influence the general east-to-west progression?
6. Designing a better One Health surveillance system: Based on all analyses in this chapter, what additional data streams or research infrastructures would improve our ability to interpret WNV dynamics? Consider environmental data (e.g., temperature, precipitation), vector surveillance, wildlife host movement, and human case data. How would integrating these datasets change the conclusions you could draw about WNV dynamics?
